rows.source: Militia Command Structure: People's Armed Forces System, Dual-Responsibility System, County-Level and Grassroots PAFDs, 2013 White Paper's 'Assistant and Backup Force of the PLA' (pp. 2–5)
rows.usage: Establishes that the militia is a reserve component distinct from PLA reserve units, funded by provincial governments and commanded by PLA military districts, subdistricts and PAFDs under local Party–military 'dual leadership.'
rows.finding: Consistent with the cited sources (`ok`): the 2013 defense white paper does describe the militia as 'an assistant and backup force of the PLA,' and the militia/reserve distinction and the county-level (active-duty) versus grassroots (civilian cadre) PAFD split are as described in standard accounts of the PRC mobilization system; the Chinese-language sources behind Notes 5–11 were not re-retrieved.

rows.source: Hainan Order-of-Battle Extrapolation: 31 PAFMM Units × (~120 Personnel, ~10 Vessels) = ~3,720 Personnel and ~310 Vessels (p. 18)
rows.usage: Offers a rough, explicitly hypothetical size estimate for the Hainan militia from the number of identified units.
rows.finding: Arithmetic verified (`ok`): 31 × 120 = 3,720 and 31 × 10 = 310. The estimate rests on an assumed median company size and omits smaller elements and outpost units the note itself mentions, so it is an order-of-magnitude illustration rather than a count; the underlying identification of 31 units could not be independently checked.

rows.source: Incident Record: USNS Impeccable (March 2009), CNOOC Survey off Triton Island (April 2013), Scarborough Shoal (10 April 2012), Second Thomas Shoal Blockade (February 2014), HYSY-981 (2014), MH370 Search (March 2014) (pp. 8–10)
rows.usage: Uses a set of well-known South China Sea incidents to show where militia vessels took part and which agencies initiated them.
rows.finding: Public-record facts match (`ok`): the March 2009 Impeccable harassment, the 10 April 2012 arrival of the Philippine ship Gregorio del Pilar at Scarborough and the 2014 HYSY-981 standoff are established events, and the Tanmen detail (six boats in the lagoon; squad leaders Chen Zebo and Xu Detan; 510 'valuable intelligence' reports) comes from Chinese-language local reporting that was not re-retrieved. The authors themselves state that available sources do not reveal a direct PLA link to the initial Scarborough encounters.

rows.source: Central Claim: Deliberate Militia Participation in Sea Incidents Occurs 'Directly Under the PLA Chain of Command, at Least in a Supervisory Capacity' (Key Points 4–5; Nature of PLA Control, pp. 2, 8–10)
rows.usage: Draws the policy conclusion that the PAFMM is 'a state-organized, -developed, and -controlled force' operating under a military chain of command, so that its actions should be attributed to the PLA.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The report's PDF p. 10 expressly says the degree of PLA involvement in the Impeccable harassment remains unclear. Its organization discussion also acknowledges uncertainty after the military-region reforms. These qualifications matter: statutory or organizational supervision of militia does not establish who issued incident-specific orders. The open question is command attribution for particular encounters, not whether the militia has a military institutional relationship. No incident order, authenticated command log or independently corroborated participant account has been recovered in this continuation.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** Incident-specific command records or independently corroborated participant evidence.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Plausible but not independently confirmed (`unk`): the structural argument (PAFD-to-military-district command lines, PLAN training, mandated communications suites) is documented from Chinese open sources, but the evidence for PLA direction in specific incidents is circumstantial — the text says the PLA's role in the Impeccable harassment is 'still unclear' and that no direct link to the initial Scarborough encounters is visible — and the Chinese sources could not be retrieved to test the inference.

paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CMR-1 — China's Third Sea Force: The People's Armed Forces Maritime Militia (Conor M. Kennedy & Andrew S. Erickson, March 2017)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: China Maritime Report No. 1 argues that the militia vessels seen in South China Sea incidents are not 'merely fishermen' but a state-organized **People's Armed Forces Maritime Militia (PAFMM)** — a 'Third Sea Force' alongside the PLAN and the coast guard — that is legally separate from the PLA yet organized, trained and commanded by the PLA's local military commands. The ambiguity is deliberate: it lets Beijing act below the threshold of PLA involvement while keeping a military chain of command, and an elite tier of professionalized 'leading units' (Danzhou, Tanmen, Sanya, Sansha) is increasingly the front line. The report is built entirely from Chinese-language open sources.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Summary and Key Points (pp. 1–2)**: Identity, name and five key points.
• **Command and Control (pp. 2–6)**: Militia versus reserves, the dual-responsibility system, PAFDs, Specialized Naval Militia Detachments, 'joint defense,' the value of ambiguity; Figure 1 (organization chart).
• **Nature of PLA Control in Specific Incidents (pp. 8–10)**: Non-PLA-initiated tasks versus PLA-initiated operations; Scarborough 2012 as the model case.
• **Key Actors: The Leading Units (pp. 10–11)**: Danzhou, Tanmen, Sanya and Sansha.
• **Appendices**: Photographs and the authors' bibliography; notes (including the Hainan estimate in Note 4).

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Concepts**: *Third Sea Force*, *People's Armed Forces Maritime Militia (PAFMM)*, *People's Armed Forces System* (人武系统), *dual-responsibility system* (双重领导), *joint military, law enforcement and civilian defense* (军警民联防), *Specialized Naval Militia Detachments*, *Three Warfares*.
• **Quantitative claims**: `31` Hainan PAFMM units identified; `~120` personnel and `~10` vessels per median company (hypothetical `3,720` personnel and `310` vessels); `510` 'valuable intelligence' reports credited to the Tanmen militia; Tanmen established `1985`; Xi's visit `April 2013`; Sansha vessels up to `59 m × 9 m` (`~750 t`), smaller `~600 t`; `$6 million` command center.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 5 reference rows audited in `CMR-01`, 4 are rated `ok` and 1 is rated `unk`; no substantive `fix` was found:
• **`[CMR01-R04]` (`unk` — PLA Chain-of-Command Claim)**: The structural case is well documented, but incident-level evidence of PLA direction is circumstantial by the authors' own account.
• **`[CMR01-R02]` (`ok`)**: The Hainan estimate is arithmetically sound but hypothetical.

The report is the **founding open-source treatment of the PAFMM** in this corpus and sets up the militia's later role in the gray-zone, coast-guard and civil-transport studies (`CMS-15`, `CMGZ-00`, `CMGZ-P1`). Its main limitation is the one it states: Chinese-language local reporting is read to infer command relationships that Beijing does not publicly spell out, and its Sansha and outpost details date from 2016–17.

**Footnote rows**: all 36 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 27 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMR01-N001 to CMR01-N036). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 36 notes: 2 (6%) are confirmed, 1 of them against a retrieved source and 1 after an outside web search (1 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 34 (94%) are not confirmed. Of the 34 notes not confirmed, 16 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 5 were judged not web-checkable (2 the authors' own data, imagery or analysis; 1 private interview or conversation; 2 notes that are explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation); 13 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 27 source rows are 2 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 25 `unk`. 12 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

rows.source: HYSY 981 (May–July 2014): '88-Day Operation,' CMP Cutters from Many Detachments as the 'Main Force,' PLA Navy Forced to Take Tactical Command (pp. 15, 21–22)
rows.usage: Presents the 2014 rig defense as the event that convinced Chinese leaders to put armed police-type forces on the front line.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The supplied report, PDF p. 17, does use an 88-day operation and describes deployment of CMP vessels from several provinces. That verifies the author's wording, not the start and end dates represented by the total. Counting the publicly visible rig standoff alone cannot exclude earlier preparation or later protection duties. The 88-day interval and the inference that the navy was forced to assume tactical command remain separate evidentiary questions. No operational calendar or direct command-transfer record is established by the passage reviewed here.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** The cited protection-operation calendar and evidence of the claimed command transfer, rather than a calculation from rig arrival and departure alone.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Partly verified; headline duration not confirmed (`unk`): the 2014 standoff south of Triton Island and Chinese water-cannon use are well documented, but public accounts date the rig's deployment from early May to its withdrawal in mid-July (about 75 days), whereas the report's '88-day operation' appears to come from a Chinese-language coast guard source (Note 46) that may count from the start of preparatory deployments. The claims that CMP cutters were the 'main force' and that the PLAN 'was forced to take tactical command' (Note 58) are the author's inferences from Chinese sources and could not be independently confirmed.

paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CMR-2 — The Arming of China's Maritime Frontier (Ryan D. Martinson, June 2017)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: China Maritime Report No. 2 explains a quiet but consequential shift in how China uses its coast guard. Until about 2013 Beijing kept its armed coast guard force (the China Maritime Police, CMP) away from disputed waters and put unarmed civilian cutters (China Marine Surveillance and Fisheries Law Enforcement) on the front line, because 'white hulls' backed by a strong military could pursue claims 'without risking an armed clash, sullying China's reputation, or provoking military intervention.' After the 2013 reform created the China Coast Guard, the armed, active-duty CMP moved to the front line, received a blue-water fleet and became the model for the whole service, a change Martinson ties to Xi Jinping's more assertive maritime policy and to the HYSY 981 conflict of 2014.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **The Age of the Toothless 'Dragons' (pp. 2–8)**: Law enforcement as an instrument of sovereignty since the 1980s; the CMP's organization, missions and fleet; Operation South China Sea (2006).
• **Coast Guard Reform (pp. 8–10)**: 'Five dragons managing the sea,' the 2013 integration plan and its slow progress (Table 1: CMP detachments by contingent).
• **Moving to the Front Line (pp. 10–16)**: CMP operations in the East China Sea (Senkakus, 2015–16; Table 2) and South China Sea (Spratlys, Scarborough, HYSY 981).
• **Acquiring a Blue-Water Fleet (pp. 15–17)**: Transfers and new classes (Table 3); CMS ships reassigned (Table 4).
• **Recruitment and 'Why the CMP?' (pp. 19–24)**: PAP commissions (Table 5), combat power, criminal-law enforcement authority, and the shift in political priorities under Xi.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Concepts**: *white hulls*, *five dragons managing the sea* (五龙制海), *China Coast Guard integration* (整合) versus unification, *active-duty China Coast Guard forces* (中国海警现役部队), *rights protection* (维权), *rights protection and stability maintenance* trade-off.
• **Quantitative claims**: CMP `>10,000` personnel and `~two dozen` detachments before reform; `>20` Type 618B cutters (`600 t`, `30 mm`); Operation South China Sea `12` cutters, `560` soldiers, `8` leased ships (1 June–31 July 2006); `>200` trawlers and `~20` law enforcement ships including `9` CMP cutters (August 2016); `88`-day HYSY 981 operation; Type 718 `2,700 t`, Type 818 `>4,000 t` with `76 mm` guns; `16` large cutters delivered since 2014; `>1,000` PAP-commissioned coast guard officers; `>300` graduates in January 2017.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 7 reference rows audited in `CMR-02`, 6 are rated `ok` and 1 is rated `unk`; no substantive `fix` was found:
• **`[CMR02-R05]` (`unk` — HYSY 981 Duration and Command)**: The '88-day' figure differs from the roughly 75 days usually cited, and the claims that CMP cutters were the 'main force' and that the PLAN took tactical command rest on Chinese-language sources that could not be retrieved.
• **Table extraction**: Tables 2 and 4 are interleaved in the extracted text and could be checked only by row count.

The study is the **clearest early account of the coast guard's militarization**: its central prediction — that the China Coast Guard would be reorganized on the model of the armed police — was borne out when the CCG was transferred to the People's Armed Police in July 2018 and given explicit authority to use weapons in 2021. It complements `CMS-15` (the white-hull / gray-hull division of labor) and `CMS-05` (the earlier 'five dragons' study), and its main limitation is its reliance on Chinese-language personnel and ship notices that the author reads as evidence of intent.

**Footnote rows**: all 71 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 65 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMR02-S1N001 to CMR02-N077). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 71 notes: 15 (21%) are confirmed, 3 of them against a retrieved source and 12 after an outside web search (11 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 3 are flagged for reader check; 56 (79%) are not confirmed. Of the 56 notes not confirmed, 30 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 9 were judged not web-checkable (2 the authors' own data, imagery or analysis; 5 notes that are explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation; 2 other items); 17 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 65 source rows are 13 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 52 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMR02-N014`: The sentence says two former Type 053H frigates were transferred to the CMP from the PLA Navy in December 2006. Wikipedia-derived pages found say the transfer occurred in 2007 and was reported in March 2007, with the same 1002 and 1003 numbers; no primary source or exact December date was retrieved; `CMR02-N039`: The sentence describes a January 2017 Spratly patrol by hull 46115. The search found no report of it; the nearest result was an AMTI photograph of a different cutter (46112) at Subi Reef in December 2017. The Beijing TV report cited could not be retrieved; `CMR02-N049`: The sentence says the CMP received two former PLA Navy frigates in late 2006. Wikipedia-derived pages found say the transfer was in 2007 (reported March 2007); no primary source was retrieved to settle the date. 25 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

The text mislabels the Qianlong 2 as a 'UAV' where an autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) is meant, as the report itself says elsewhere. The '250 million km²' high seas figure is Liu Cigui's own rounded phrase as quoted by the authors.

rows.source: Civil-Military Support to the PLAN: Nine-Ship Type 636 Haiyang Survey Fleet ('More Than Tripled Since 2015'), January 2009 MLR–PLAN Agreement, 2009 and April 2017 SOA–PLAN Agreements, 'Transparent Ocean' Network (pp. 10–13)
rows.usage: Argues that civilian oceanography is organized to support the navy's mastery of the 'ocean battlespace environment' and that some cruises are effectively military surveys.
rows.finding: Supported with a counting slip (`ok · slip`): the agreements and the Transparent Ocean project are documented with Chinese-language sources (Notes 47, 50, 55–56) not re-retrieved, and the authors acknowledge integration is 'far from perfect' (Zhang Haiwen, March 2018). The table of Haiyang-class ships lists three through 2015 and nine by 2018, which is exactly tripled rather than 'more than tripled,' and the claim that cruises are 'military surveys' is an inference from integration, not a documented tasking.

rows.source: Maritime Diplomacy and Access: Haiyang 6 to the Eastern Pacific (March 2013), June 2017 Vision for Maritime Cooperation, Shiyan 1 in Colombo (18–22 April 2016), Xiang Yang Hong 10 Surveys of Mozambique and Seychelles (June 2016), Qingdao Lab–Maldives Cruises (2015, 2017) (pp. 13–15)

rows.source: Implications and Caveats: Quality Still Trails the U.S. (Yang Desen, Da Lianglong), 2015 Science of Military Strategy and July 2015 National Security Law on Seabed Interests, Seabed Contracts East of Guam and Southeast of Hawaii as a Naval Rationale (pp. 15–17)
rows.usage: Weighs Chinese limitations against the strategic implications, concluding that survey activity is a leading indicator of far-seas naval presence.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The legal component is now directly corroborated: Article 32 of the July 1, 2015 National Security Law explicitly refers to safeguarding China's activities, assets and other interests in international seabed areas, alongside outer space and polar regions. The authorized text is available in the Cyberspace Administration's contemporary republication. It does not assert that a particular seabed contract requires a naval deployment. The report's could-justify formulation on PDF p. 18 remains a scenario advanced by the authors. The separate translated scientific-quality criticisms and the contracts' precise geographic scope still require their own originals.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** Original scientific self-assessment passages and contract locators; evidence for any asserted causal connection to a particular naval-presence decision.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Partly speculative (`unk`): the quoted Chinese complaints about derivative research and the 2015 National Security Law text on 'international seabed areas' are sourced to Chinese publications that could not be retrieved, and the forward-looking claim that seabed contracts 'could justify' a bolstered naval presence east of Guam and southeast of Hawaii is the authors' own scenario, with no Chinese statement to that effect cited.

rows.source: Xuelong’s return to Shanghai after its 2017 Arctic expedition
rows.usage: The note is attached to: “It transited Japan’s Tsugaru Strait on October 4th, arriving in Shanghai four days later.”
rows.finding: The expedition partner’s record ends on 10 October 2017, consistent with contemporaneous reporting of the ship’s Shanghai return. Four days after the paper’s stated 4 October passage would be 8 October. Use 10 October for the documented Shanghai return and verify the earlier passage date independently before giving an elapsed time.

rows.source: High-seas water column versus the international seabed Area
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMR03-N007: The source note defines high seas as waters outside coastal-state jurisdiction while the attached passage describes COMRA exploration of seabed resources.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 11, 2026. Terminology needs separation. Article 86 excludes the EEZ, territorial sea, internal waters and archipelagic waters from Part VII. Article 1(1)(1) separately defines the international seabed Area by limits of national jurisdiction. Water-column status does not itself determine seabed status, including where a continental shelf extends farther. The treaty check supports this distinction; it does not establish COMRA founding dates or the legal status of individual contract sites. Rechecked November 14, 2026. Articles 76 and 78 confirm that extended shelf rights can coexist with a distinct legal status of the water column. Use Area when describing seabed beyond national jurisdiction. Confirm any site-specific characterization from the relevant contract and shelf entitlement records. Follow-up review, November 14, 2026. Correct any reading that treats high-seas water-column status as the legal status of the underlying seabed. Articles 1, 76, 78 and 86 distinguish these concepts. This finding concerns treaty terminology and does not decide where an individual seabed concession lies.

rows.source: Article 246 consent conditions are not a definition of MSR
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMR03-N058: The passage presents research benefiting mankind as the UNCLOS definition of marine scientific research and contrasts it with military data collection.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 11, 2026. Article 246(3) states the circumstances in which coastal States should normally consent to research projects; it does not define the term marine scientific research. Article 246(5)(a) also contemplates research directly significant for resource exploration or exploitation. Correct the definitional attribution. The treaty alone does not settle how the described cruises should be classified, and their actual tasking remains unverified.

rows.source: Coastal participation rights do not guarantee foreign research access
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMR03-N066: Marine-science cooperation is said to ensure Chinese access to strategically important parts of other States’ EEZs; the note cites the coastal State’s participation right.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 11, 2026. Article 249(1)(a) protects participation by the coastal State, at its desire and when practicable, in research in its own EEZ or shelf. It does not guarantee access to a visiting research State. Article 246 retains the coastal consent regime. The article supports a cooperation mechanism, while guaranteed Chinese access remains an inference requiring project agreements or permits. No such permit was examined. Rechecked November 14, 2026. Article 249 conditions coastal-state participation on its desire and practicability. Article 247 has a separate rule for projects under qualifying international organizations. Neither is a general guarantee for a partner’s foreign research vessel. The claimed practical effect remains to be tested against individual authorizations. Follow-up review, November 14, 2026. Article 249 describes how a coastal State may participate in research within its own EEZ or on its shelf. Article 246 governs consent. Revise any inference that research cooperation guarantees visiting-State access. Separate that legal point from whether particular projects obtained permission.

rows.source: Broader naval missions in the April 2013 defense white paper
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMR03-N040. The navy came to embrace a wider set of noncombat missions after concentrating on war preparation and deterrence.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The 2013 white paper explicitly includes merchant-shipping protection and international cooperation alongside traditional defense and combat readiness. That verifies a broadened publicly stated mission set. It does not measure when operational priorities changed or how far earlier practice differed. The other cited Wu Shengli/Liu Xiaojiang writings remain separate evidence for the chapter’s historical interpretation.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** The relevant earlier statements and dated historical practice for the claimed change in emphasis.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Reviewed November 13, 2026. The paper describes merchant shipping protection and cooperation as roles alongside combat readiness and traditional defense tasks. It supports a broadened stated mission set. The point at which priorities changed and the degree of earlier emphasis require the other cited writings and evidence of practice.
evidence: 2013 white paper, sections III–V on missions and international cooperation

paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CMR-3 — China's Distant-Ocean Survey Activities: Implications for U.S. National Security (Ryan D. Martinson & Peter A. Dutton, November 2018)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: China Maritime Report No. 3 explains why China sends 5–10 oceanographic research vessels to distant waters on any given day. Martinson and Dutton argue that the activity is driven mainly by the search for seabed minerals in international waters and by the PLAN's need to understand the ocean environment in the Philippine Sea and Indian Ocean, with diplomacy a secondary purpose; because China's civilian research and military oceanography are tightly integrated, U.S. analysts cannot easily separate science from naval preparation. The report is a baseline for later work on the PLA's marine environment support and undersea sensor programs.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Fleet Composition (pp. 2–4)**: MNR, CAS, COMRA and university ships; the National Marine Research Fleet (Table 1) and China Geological Survey ships (Table 2).
• **Primary Operating Areas (pp. 4–6)**: Near-seas history and the 2017 out-of-area snapshot; the First–Second Island Chain zone; four ISA contract zones (Table 3).
• **Types of Research Activities (pp. 6–8)**: Sensors, moorings, submersibles, AUVs and gliders.
• **Strategic Purposes (pp. 8–15)**: Seabed resources; naval strategy and civil-military integration; maritime diplomacy.
• **Implications (pp. 15–17)**: Scale of investment, marine science as a pillar of naval power, integration, quality gap, leading indicator of far-seas presence.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Concepts**: *distant-ocean* (远洋) operations, *scientific research vessel* (科学考查船), *National Marine Research Fleet*, *ocean battlespace environment* (海战场环境), *military oceanography*, *Transparent Ocean* project, *maritime power* (海洋强国), *marine scientific research* versus *military survey* under UNCLOS.
• **Quantitative claims**: `19` vessels in the National Fleet (2012), `50` by end-2017 (half distant-ocean capable), `10` more in design; `5–10` vessels out of area on any day, `11` in October 2017; `4` ISA contract zones with `15`-year terms; COMRA's `10,000 km²` Southwest Indian Ocean zone; XYH 10 `250`-day cruise, Qianlong 2 `9` dives / `257` hours; Project 908 `30,000+` personnel, `8+` years; Type 636 Haiyang fleet `3` → `9` ships; UNOLS `9` large ships.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 6 reference rows audited in `CMR-03`, 5 are rated `ok` (two with slips) and 1 is rated `unk`; no substantive `fix` was found:
• **`[CMR03-R03]` (`ok · slip`)**: The Qianlong 2 AUV is mislabeled a 'UAV.'
• **`[CMR03-R04]` (`ok · slip`)**: The PLAN survey fleet is described as 'more than tripled' but the table shows an exact tripling (3 to 9).
• **`[CMR03-R06]` (`unk`)**: The naval-protection rationale for seabed contracts is a scenario, not a documented Chinese position.

The report is the **standard open-source baseline on China's civilian ocean-science fleet** and its link to naval requirements; it sets the stage for the PLA marine-environment translations (`CMSI-70`) and for the undersea-sensing and gray-zone discussions in `CMGZ-P1` and `CIPI-DS26`. Its limitations are that fleet tables are partly image-based and that many Chinese-language sources on civil-military agreements were not retrievable.

**Footnote rows**: all 81 footnotes were extracted and added to the Reference Audit Matrix as source rows (CMR03-N001 to CMR03-N081), each with its citing sentence and the result of the check. Footnote-level result: 81 notes: 19 (23%) are confirmed, 2 of them against a retrieved source and 17 after an outside web search (11 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 1 is flagged for reader check; 62 (77%) are not confirmed. Of the 62 notes not confirmed, 36 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 6 were judged not web-checkable (2 the authors' own data, imagery or analysis; 1 print-only book or paywalled item; 3 notes that are explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation); 20 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 81 source rows are 19 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 62 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMR03-N015`: The sentence says the Snow Dragon passed Japan's Tsugaru Strait on October 4 and reached Shanghai four days later (about October 8); China Daily's October 11, 2017 report says it docked in Shanghai on Tuesday (October 10). 17 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

sections.heading: Open claim-audit follow-up, November 22, 2026 (review complete; gaps recorded)
sections.body:
This continuation targets 2 initially open claim audits in this paper. 2 have a recorded individual follow-up: 0 now have a supported or correction finding; 2 remain unresolved. 0 of this paper’s initial open audits still await this continuation. Every reviewed row retains its evidence limits; a completed follow-up does not mean every substantive claim is verified.

rows.source: Strategic Projection Timeline: Liu Jiasheng's Three Phases (February 2019, Short / Medium / Long Term) and the Definition of 'Strategic Projection' (pp. 2–4)
rows.usage: Frames the PLA's civil-transport developments as a response to an explicit three-phase requirement set by the CMC Transport and Projection Bureau.
rows.finding: Consistent with the cited source (`ok`): the three phases and the Chinese-language terms are given with quotations from Liu Jiasheng's February 2019 article in the Journal of Military Transportation University; the article itself could not be re-retrieved, and the report's other cited sources (the 2011 PLA Dictionary of Military Terms, the 2013 and 2015 Science of Military Strategy volumes) are standard references.

rows.source: Strategic Projection Support Ship Fleets: 63 RO-RO Ships Totaling 140,000 Tons, Bohai Ferry Group (11 Ferries, 20,000–35,000 Tons, 200–300 Vehicles, Bohai Cuizhu 2012), Hainan Strait Shipping (165,633 Tons Displacement), CSC RORO Logistics (25 Car Carriers, Changdalong 20,000 Tons) (pp. 6–11)
rows.usage: Quantifies the civilian RO-RO capacity organized into transport dadui for PLA use.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The wording on PDF p. 9 is 63 civilian RO-RO ships suitable for military use, totaling 140,000 tons in capacity. It does not call the 140,000 figure displacement. The earlier comparison with the displacement of eleven large ferries therefore does not establish an internal numerical contradiction. The precise capacity measure and sample date still need Li Peng, Sun Hao and Zhao Xiqing's article cited in note 31. The company-level fleet populations cannot be assumed to equal that selected suitable-ship population. Retain the figure as an attributed estimate pending the original passage and unit definition.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** Original note-31 passage, capacity unit, census date and the inclusion list for the 63 selected ships.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Partly confirmed; headline total is ambiguous (`unk`): the company-level details (ferry sizes and vehicle capacities, the 2012 Bohai Cuizhu with PLA-influenced design, the Hainan Strait fleet's 165,633 displacement tons and 32,571 tons of cargo capacity, the 25-ship CSC RORO fleet) are given with company websites and Chinese military articles and are internally consistent, but the '63 ships, 140,000 tons' figure from a PLA journal cannot be reconciled with the company figures (eleven Bohai ferries alone are 20,000–35,000 tons each) unless it measures a different quantity, and the report does not say which.

rows.source: Civil RO-RO Exercises: PLAAF Units Over >1,000 nm (Summer 2015, 20,000-Ton Ship), 15,000-Ton Ship in November 2017 and 2019, Northern Theater Ammunition Delivery (September 2016), PLANMC Crossing of the Bohai Gulf with Nine Ferries (July 2019), Rail-Ferry Shipment from West Lüshun to Yantai (August 2016) (pp. 10–12, 24–26)
rows.usage: Documents the use of civil ferries in actual PLA movements of air, ground and naval-infantry units.
rows.finding: Consistent with the cited PLA Daily, China Military Online and PLA Pictorial reporting (`ok`): the exercise dates, ship sizes and the route lengths are as reported in these Chinese sources, which could not be re-retrieved; the report appropriately notes that the 2015 exercise's disembarkation port 'is unknown.' The 2019 PLANMC movement of armor, artillery and vehicles over the Bohai on civilian and rail ferries is consistent with later reconstructions of 2025 exercises in `CMR-52`, which show the same class of ferries at work.

rows.source: Container and Other Civil Fleets: COSCO Shipping Corporation's 497 Container Ships and Over Three Million TEU, Third-Largest Carrier in the World (pp. 12–14)
rows.usage: Illustrates the scale of civilian container shipping that the PLA could draw on for cargo.
rows.finding: Consistent with industry reporting for 2019 (`ok`): COSCO Shipping was then ranked third behind Maersk and MSC with a capacity in the neighborhood of three million TEU, and the 497-ship figure is attributed to company materials (Note 55) that were not re-retrieved; the report's cautious wording ('it stands to reason that the PLA…') makes clear that PLA use of container fleets is inferred.

rows.source: Civil Aviation Reserve: 3,160 Passenger Aircraft and 143 Cargo Aircraft in 2017, 1.6 Percent Domestically Produced, First Strategic Projection Support Aircraft Fleet (China Southern, 2013) and 15 More (pp. 14–21)
rows.usage: Describes how PLA experts count civil airlift and how commercial airlines were organized into support fleets.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** CAAC's 2017 statistical bulletin, printed p. 8 / PDF p. 10, gives 3,296 registered civil transport aircraft at year end. The report's 3,160 passenger plus 143 cargo aircraft sum to 3,303, so they do not equal that official snapshot. This is a seven-aircraft difference, not proof that one source is false without matching date and scope. The report's PDF p. 21 separately states 1.6 percent domestic production and describes 2013 and later support fleets; CAAC's aggregate count supplies no basis for those claims. Their original expert and organizational records remain necessary.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** A matching-date fleet-type table, aircraft-origin definition, and dated creation records for the civil aviation support fleets.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Plausible but not matched to an official source (`unk`): the aircraft counts and the 1.6 percent domestic-production share are attributed to PLA experts (Notes 86–89) and are consistent in magnitude with Civil Aviation Administration of China statistics, but the report cites no CAAC table and the figures could not be tied to one in this pass; the 2013 China Southern fleet and the 'fifteen more' fleets rest on Chinese-language PLA and company reports. Follow-up review, November 15, 2026. CAAC’s statistical bulletin reports 3,296 registered civil transport aircraft at end-2017. This supplies an official reference total. The report’s split and production share require a comparable fleet date and definitions for aircraft origin and type. Source recheck. The CAAC June 2017 meeting reports 3,065 civil transport aircraft, and its year-end account reports 3,296, separately from 2,292 general-aviation aircraft. The chapter’s passenger-plus-cargo sum is 3,303. It cannot be identified with either official snapshot. The CAAC releases do not corroborate the aircraft-origin percentage.
evidence: CAAC mid-2017 meeting with fleet date
CAAC, 2017 statistical bulletin, transport fleet total on PDF p. 10

rows.source: Rail, Road and Projection Bases: Truck Fleets (First Established July 2013, Xinjiang), About 100 Low-Flatbed Trucks of 40 Tons or More Nationwide, Rail-Ferry Links, Zhengzhou Strategic Projection Base (2014) (pp. 22–29)
rows.usage: Shows heavy-equipment trucking as a bottleneck and the first projection base as a test of civil-military logistics integration.
rows.finding: Consistent with the cited Chinese sources (`ok`): the July 2013 Xinjiang fleet, the roughly 100 large low-flatbed trucks and the Zhengzhou base are documented in PLA and trade journals; the comparison with a U.S. ratio of one transport vehicle for every seven units of heavy equipment is a Chinese officer's characterization of the U.S. system and was not independently checked. The report dates the Zhengzhou base to 2014 while its own note records development from 2011 and work from February 2012.

rows.source: Challenges: Outdated Standards, Lax Training, Operational Security Lapses, Unclear Command and Activation Authority between Theater Command Offices and the JLSF, CMC Joint Transport Simulation Project (pp. 29–34)
rows.usage: Qualifies the capability narrative by showing the problems Chinese authors themselves identify.
rows.finding: Consistent with the cited PLA journal articles (`ok`): the criticisms of standards, training, secrecy and command authority are paraphrased from PLA authors (Notes 141–149) rather than observed by the report, and the 2019 CMC project on a 'Planning, Command, and Simulation Platform for Transport and Projection in Joint Operations' is described as expected to finish by the end of 2019 with no outcome reported.

rows.source: Bali evacuation: interim passenger totals and fleet attribution
rows.usage: Note 103 reports that strategic projection support aircraft evacuated 17,000 Chinese nationals from Bali in November 2017.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The CAAC account and December 4 Xinhua report concern the same Bali emergency but use interim and final return totals. The latter identifies nearly 14,000 returns by a December cutoff, rather than 17,000 in November. Both describe civil-airline activity; neither assigns all passengers to the strategic-projection-support fleet category. Without the original fleet-specific record, a different cutoff or broader evacuation definition cannot be ruled out.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** The original 17,000 passenger series and flight-to-fleet attribution, with dates and treatment of alternate departure airports.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** CAAC’s dated account distinguishes 1,658 passengers returned by domestic airlines and 2,893 returned by international airlines by 09:30 on November 30, with additional flights planned. These are interim returns, not a final total. It names civilian carriers but does not establish which flights belonged to a strategic projection support fleet. The earlier flag also omitted the domestic-airline subtotal. Retrieve Zhang et al., p. 6 and a final evacuation tally before accepting or rejecting the 17,000 figure or fleet attribution. Consistency review, November 14, 2026. The dated CAAC notice is an interim tally for both Chinese and international carriers. The two reported subtotals sum to 4,551 by the stated cutoff. Use the same event-specific attribution as CMS10-R13. This does not determine the final exit count or which carriers worked in a specially designated fleet. Follow-up review, November 14, 2026. December 4 reporting indicates nearly 14,000 travellers had returned by then. That is a later interim estimate, not a final tally. The specific claim of 17,000 and the named fleet attribution remain open pending the cited journal article or the final passenger series. Follow-up review, November 15, 2026. The CAAC update’s two carrier totals add to 4,551 by the stated cutoff, which is an interim subtotal. A later final bulletin would need to show the relevant reporting window and how any subset of these flights was assigned to the organizations described. Source recheck. The later press account attributes an aggregate of nearly 14,000 returns to the Chinese consular response by the stated December cutoff. That broad return figure covers a different interval from the CAAC’s interim figures. It still cannot substantiate 17,000 at the November cutoff or assign the total to a particular fleet.
evidence: China Overseas Chinese Network, December 4 reported return total

paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CMR-4 — Civil Transport in PLA Power Projection (Conor M. Kennedy, December 2019)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: China Maritime Report No. 4 shows how the PLA is covering a shortfall in its own strategic lift by contracting civilian carriers into 'strategic projection support forces.' Kennedy argues that since 2012 the PLA has organized RO-RO, container, tanker and semi-submersible ships, commercial aircraft fleets, rail and truck operators into numbered ship and aircraft 'fleets,' backed by the 2016 National Defense Transportation Law and a first strategic projection base at Zhengzhou. The planning is explicit — a three-phase timeline from a regional informatized war to 'global projection' — but the PLA also admits gaps in standards, training, secrecy and command authority.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Strategic Projection Needs (pp. 2–4)**: Definition, East Asian and overseas drivers, the three-phase plan.
• **Organizing Civilian Carriers (pp. 4–6)**: Legal basis and PLA organization.
• **Strategic Sea Lift (pp. 6–14)**: RO-RO fleets and exercises, container fleets, other ship types.
• **Strategic Airlift (pp. 14–21)**: Civil aviation reserve and support aircraft fleets.
• **Rail and Road Projection (pp. 22–28)**: Rail-ferry links, truck fleets, heavy-equipment shortages.
• **Strategic Projection Bases (pp. 28–29)**: Zhengzhou.
• **Challenges and Conclusion (pp. 29–34)**: Standards, training, operational security, PLA jointness and command.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Concepts**: *strategic projection* (战略投送), *strategic projection support forces* (战略投送支援力量), *strategic projection support ship fleet* (战略投送支援船队), *transport dadui* (海运大队), *civil-military fusion*, *strategic projection base* (战略投送基地), *National Defense Transportation Law*, *informatized local war*.
• **Quantitative claims**: `63` civilian RO-RO ships (`140,000 t` capacity); Bohai Ferry Group `11` ferries (`20,000–35,000 t`, `200–300` vehicles); Hainan Strait fleet `165,633 t`; CSC RORO `25` car carriers; COSCO `497` container ships (`>3 million TEU`); `3,160` passenger and `143` cargo aircraft (2017); first aircraft fleet `2013` and `15` more; first truck fleet `July 2013`; about `100` flatbeds of `40 t` or more; Zhengzhou base `2014`.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 7 reference rows audited in `CMR-04`, 5 are rated `ok` and 2 are rated `unk`; no substantive `fix` was found:
• **`[CMR04-R02]` (`unk` — RO-RO Capacity)**: The '63 ships, 140,000 tons' figure cannot be reconciled with the company-level displacement figures and its unit is not stated.
• **`[CMR04-R05]` (`unk` — Civil Aviation Counts)**: The aircraft totals come from PLA experts and were not matched to CAAC statistics.

The report is the **foundational English-language account of PLA reliance on civilian carriers** and can be compared with Chinese-source material on sealift and RO-RO use in this corpus (`CMSI-63`, `CMSI-65`, `CMSI-66`) including the earlier CMSI-65 (2016) and later proposals; it also provides context for the 2025 exercise reconstruction in `CMR-52`. Its limits are that almost all evidence is from Chinese-language promotional and professional sources and that the figures are 2017–2019 snapshots.

**Footnote rows**: all 156 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 112 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMR04-N001 to CMR04-N152). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 156 notes: 27 (17%) are confirmed, 6 of them against a retrieved source and 21 after an outside web search (19 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 2 are flagged for reader check; 129 (83%) are not confirmed. Of the 129 notes not confirmed, 106 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 1 was judged not web-checkable (1 note that is explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation); 22 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 112 source rows are 23 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 89 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMR04-N100`: The sentence says four PLAAF Il-76 aircraft from the Guangzhou Military Region and a Type 054A frigate from the 7th Escort Task Force were sent, and that over 35,000 Chinese in Libya were evacuated, partly by ground to Tunisia; `CMR04-N103`: The sentence says that during the November 2017 Mount Agung eruption aircraft of the strategic projection support aircraft fleet reportedly evacuated 17,000 Chinese nationals from Ngurah Rai airport. 29 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

rows.source: Evolution and Fabrication: 2009 Approval, 2014 Start at Jiangnan, ~29-Month Build, 6 Billion RMB (~$852 Million), Launch of Nanchang on 28 June 2017, Eight Hulls in Build, Six Type 052C, ~24 Type 052D Expected by 2025 (pp. 3–6)
rows.usage: Traces the program from the Soviet-supplied fleet through the 052C and 052D to the Type 055 and quantifies its build rate and cost.
rows.finding: Verified against the public record and internally (`ok`): the Nanchang's launch date of 28 June 2017 and commissioning on 12 January 2020 match official reporting, the 6 billion RMB and $852 million figures are consistent at about 7 RMB per dollar, and one commissioned plus seven in fitting-out equals the eight hulls the text counts; the cost and build-time figures come from a Chinese analysis (Note 21) and are estimates.

rows.source: Size Claim: 'Exceeding 12,000 Tons… Nearly Double the Tonnage of Its Chinese Destroyer Predecessor and 23 Meters Longer' vs. the Comparison Table (Type 052D 8,500 Tons, 157 m) (pp. 2, 15)
rows.usage: Presents the Type 055's size as the key discontinuity in PLAN surface-combatant design.
rows.finding: Internal inconsistency (`fix`): the report's own comparison table lists the Type 052D at 8,500 tons, so 12,000 tons is about 1.4 times, not 'nearly double'; the '23 meters longer' claim does agree with the table (180 m versus 157 m). The 'nearly double' wording would only hold against a much smaller predecessor, and the report does not say which predecessor it means.

rows.source: Sensors and Stealth: Single Integrated Mast, Dual-Band Planar Radars, S-Band Arrays '40 Percent Larger' than the 052D with a '60 Percent' Gain in Sensing Distance, Four Stacks Enclosed, Type 364B (pp. 7–10)
rows.usage: Describes the sensor suite and its integration as the ship's revolutionary feature, citing Chinese magazine analyses.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The supplied PDF p. 10 uses reported, said and expected language for the radar comparisons. It supplies no independent test establishing the quoted range improvement or the conditions under which the magazines' figures were obtained. Array size alone cannot independently verify a whole-system comparison. The earlier audit's simplified calculation is not a measurement of either system and should not be treated as a competing tested result. The original commentary and independently documented conditions remain missing; this continuation makes no new performance estimate.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** Original cited commentary and evidence identifying the measured quantity, comparison conditions and test basis.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Not independently confirmed (`unk`): the radar claims are quoted from Chinese commentary (Notes 36–40). A 40 percent larger array area would give roughly an 18 percent increase in range at fixed power under the radar equation, so the quoted 60 percent range gain must reflect additional changes (power, processing) that the source does not specify; the Type 364B's performance and the 400 km range quoted for the 052D's Type 364A are unverified claims.

rows.source: Weapons: 112 VLS Cells (64 Forward, 48 Aft), Universal VLS, HHQ-9B and HQ-16B, Compared with 52D (64), Arleigh Burke (96), Atago (96), Zumwalt (80) and Sejong the Great (128) (pp. 11–16, 18)
rows.usage: Quantifies the magazine capacity increase and compares it with foreign large combatants.
rows.finding: Consistent with public data (`ok`): 64 + 48 = 112; the comparison values (Burke Flight IIA 96, Atago 96, Zumwalt 80, Sejong the Great 128) match standard references; the report correctly notes the Korean ship exceeds the Type 055's cell count. The universal-VLS cell dimensions and the claim that all cells can host the largest missiles rest on Chinese and U.S. open-source inference.

rows.source: Strategic Roles: Two Type 055 Among Eight Escorts in a 2017 Carrier Strike Group Sketch, Eight Hulls for Four Carrier Groups vs. 'Up to 24' in Western Sources, Possible Surface Action Group Flagship Role (pp. 16–20)
rows.usage: Infers the Type 055's missions from numbers and from Chinese graphics of carrier groups.
rows.finding: Arithmetic and logic consistent (`ok`): two of eight escorts is a quarter, and eight ships for four carrier groups follows from two per group; the 'up to 24' figure is attributed to unnamed Western sources and the surface-action-group flagship role is the authors' inference from the ship's command capacity.

rows.source: Chinese Assessments of Survivability and Parity: 'No Basis' for U.S. Claims of Submarine Vulnerability, 'Meets or Exceeds' the Burke and Atago (Li Jie, Song Zhongping), 'Cross Blend of Ticonderoga and Zumwalt' (pp. 14–19)
rows.usage: Reports Chinese expert judgments about the ship's relative quality and anti-submarine survivability.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The quoted parity and survivability judgments are expert opinions reported by the study. Their existence as reported judgments is different from the comparative performance they assert. The study's own caveat about unproven integration and reliability is material and must remain visible. No independent comparative test or evidence demonstrating the experts' underlying assessment was recovered. Keep these claims explicitly attributed and conditional rather than converting them into established combat-performance findings.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** The original expert passages and independent evidence for the asserted comparative performance, with like-for-like conditions.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Assertions rather than tests (`unk`): the quoted Chinese experts are advocates, the report itself notes that 'some maintain' that the quality of China's shipbuilding, the integration of sensors and weapons and the reliability of the missiles remain unproven (Note 102), and nothing in the report establishes the ship's combat performance; the ASW claim rests on a Chinese magazine rebuttal (Note 116).

paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CMR-5 — China's Dreadnought? The PLA Navy's Type 055 Cruiser (Daniel Caldwell, Joseph Freda & Lyle J. Goldstein, February 2020)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: China Maritime Report No. 5 is the first comprehensive open-source study of the Type 055, which the U.S. calls the Renhai-class cruiser. Caldwell, Freda and Goldstein use Chinese naval magazines and journals to argue that the ship's size, stealth, integrated sensor mast and 112-cell VLS magazine place the PLAN among the world's leading surface fleets, and that the ship's likely roles — carrier escort, air and missile defense, command platform — will expand the range and firepower of the PLAN. They suggest a 'Dreadnought moment' while acknowledging that Chinese shipbuilding integration and missile reliability remain unproven.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Introduction (pp. 1–3)**: The 'going large' (大型化) decision and first commissioning.
• **Evolution and Fabrication (pp. 3–6)**: From the 'four big diamonds' to the 052C and 052D; cost, build time, shipyards.
• **Capabilities (pp. 6–14)**: Propulsion, integrated mast, radars, sonar, weapons and VLS, helicopters.
• **Peer Comparison (pp. 14–16)**: Table against Type 052D, Arleigh Burke, Zumwalt and Atago.
• **Strategic Meaning (pp. 16–20)**: Carrier escort, flagship and other roles; implications for the U.S. Navy.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Concepts**: *going large* (大型化), *Red Aegis*, *integrated mast*, *dual-band radar*, *universal VLS*, *super destroyer club* (超级驱逐舰), *fit out a generation, build a generation, design a generation* (装备一代、生产一代、预研一代), *carrier strike group escort*.
• **Quantitative claims**: `>12,000 t`, `180 m`; `112` VLS cells (`64` forward, `48` aft) vs `64` on the 052D; build time `~29 months`; cost `~6 billion RMB` (`$852 million`); launch `28 June 2017`; commissioning `January 2020`; `8` hulls expected by `2025`; `6` Type 052C and `~24` Type 052D by 2025; S-band arrays `40%` larger; `>32 knots`; `130,000 hp`; `2` Type 055 among `8` carrier escorts.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 6 reference rows audited in `CMR-05`, 3 are rated `ok`, 2 are rated `unk` and 1 is rated `fix`:
• **`[CMR05-R02]` (`fix` — 'Nearly Double' Tonnage)**: The report's own table gives 8,500 and 12,000 tons for the 052D and 055, a ratio of about 1.4.
• **`[CMR05-R03]` (`unk` — Radar Range Gain)**: A '40 percent larger' array is quoted with a '60 percent' range gain that exceeds what area alone would give.
• **`[CMR05-R06]` (`unk` — Survivability and Parity Claims)**: Chinese assessments are asserted rather than tested.

The report is a **well-sourced first look at the Type 055** that gains weight from the later commissioning of the entire class, and it connects naturally to the carrier, escort and shipbuilding material in this corpus (`CMSI-T30`, `CMSI-86`, `CMS-14`). Its limits are the misaligned comparison table, the reliance on Chinese commentary for capability claims and the small number of independent checks.

**Footnote rows**: all 140 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 72 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMR05-N001 to CMR05-N140). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 140 notes: 45 (32%) are confirmed, 8 of them against a retrieved source and 37 after an outside web search (30 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 3 are flagged for reader check; 95 (68%) are not confirmed. Of the 95 notes not confirmed, 62 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 2 were judged not web-checkable (1 the authors' own data, imagery or analysis; 1 note that is explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation); 30 were searched on the web without finding corroboration; 1 has not been searched. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 72 source rows are 22 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 50 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMR05-N023`: The sentence says Navy commander Shen Jinlong attended the launch of the Type 055. Sources found describe the 28 June 2017 launch ceremony as presided over by Zhang Youxia and do not mention Shen, while one result places Shen at the 2020 commissioning; `CMR05-N071`: The sentence says the YJ-18 anti-ship missile has a range of 290 nautical miles, citing the 2019 Military and Security Developments report. A Washington Times article on a later Pentagon report gives the YJ-18A 250 nautical miles and attributes 290 nautical miles to the supersonic YJ-12A; other sources give shorter figures; `CMR05-N138`: The Chinese-language source (Yin He) says in 2014 the US Navy decided to build three ships of the class and the planned 32-ship programme was cancelled. English sources date the reduction to three ships to the 2009 budget announcement (earlier cuts from 32 to 24 to 7 to 3 came before the lead ship was funded in 2005 to 2008)…. 17 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

rows.source: Setting and Timeline: Maritime Lifeline Splitting at Bab-el-Mandeb, ~40 Percent of Imported Oil via Hormuz, Regularized Escorts from December 2008, Japan's 2011 Base, Chinese Port Begun 2012, Base Construction February 2016 (Introduction, pp. 2–4, 22)
rows.usage: Provides the strategic and chronological frame for China's Djibouti presence.
rows.finding: Consistent with the public record (`ok`): the December 2008 start of PLAN escort task forces, Japan's 2011 facility and the February 2016 start of base construction are widely documented; the '40 percent of imported oil' figure is attributed to the International Energy Agency (Note 7) and could not be re-checked in this pass.

rows.source: Doraleh Multipurpose Port: 23.5 Percent CMPort Stake (JV Finalized December 2012), 4-Year $590 Million Exim-Financed Project (2013–2017), Six Berths (Printed '1200 Meter'), 23 + 57 + 20 + 15 + 3.5 Hectares of Yards, 49,000 of 220,000 Designed TEU in 2018 (p. 10)
rows.usage: Describes the centerpiece Chinese commercial asset and its underused capacity.
rows.finding: Consistent with the cited company and press sources (`ok · slip`): the yard areas total 118.5 hectares and the 2018 throughput is about 22 percent of design capacity, as the text implies; the '1200 meter ship berths' wording is likely a slip for a 1,200 m quay line with six berths. The ownership share and project cost are from CMPort and Exim Bank materials not re-retrieved.

rows.source: Other Chinese Projects: Ghoubet Salt Terminal ($64 Million Exim Loan, 5 Million Tons/Year), Bulk Terminals Using 4.4 of ~20 Million Tons Capacity (2018), Free Trade Zone (2.4 km² Pilot, $370 Million of a Planned $3.5 Billion/48 km² Zone), CMPort Loans up to $150 Million (pp. 11–14)
rows.usage: Shows the breadth of Chinese commercial positions and how far actual throughput lags capacity.
rows.finding: Internally consistent (`ok`): the pilot zone is about 10.6 percent of the planned investment and 5 percent of the planned area, and the bulk-terminal utilization is about 22 percent; the figures come from CMPort annual reports and Chinese and African press (Notes 63–93) that were not re-retrieved, and the 'planned' values are promotional projections.

rows.source: Scale of Chinese Commitment: 'Estimated $15 Billion Total Chinese Investment in the Port and Its Hinterlands,' Largest External Commercial Player and Principal Creditor (p. 5)
rows.usage: Underpins the claim that China's commercial stake made the base politically feasible and gives Beijing leverage.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The report labels $15 billion an estimate on PDF p. 8. Project cost, loan commitments, creditor exposure and investment stock are different measures; a debt-sustainability account cannot simply be added to construction contracts to reproduce that total. The same estimate is separately audited in CMR06-R21, so the source comparison is shared rather than counted as a second independent check. The record still lacks the original estimator's project inventory, valuation convention and geographic perimeter. Commercial size alone also cannot establish the cause of a basing approval.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** The original $15 billion project ledger and valuation date/scope, plus direct decision evidence for the causal political claim.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Not confirmed (`unk`): the $15 billion total is presented as an estimate with a single footnoted source (Note 23) and is several times larger than the project-level figures the report itemizes elsewhere ($590 million port, $64 million salt terminal, $370 million pilot zone, $150 million loans), so it appears to include announced or planned projects as well as completed ones; the report does not reconcile the two. Follow-up review, November 15, 2026. The IMF project accounts distinguish creditor exposure from project cost and list dated commitments. Neither that ledger nor the report’s estimate establishes a causal link from commercial ownership to political approval. That link would need dated decision records or statements from the parties.

rows.source: Djibouti’s $15 billion estimate: investment, contracts and loan commitments
rows.usage: The note is attached to: “With an estimated $15 billion total Chinese investment in development of the port and its hinterlands, China is the largest external commercial player in Djibouti.”
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** This row repeats the $15 billion passage also examined in CMR06-R04, so the evidence comparison is shared. The IMF's debt-sustainability text identifies particular China Eximbank loans and their 2014–2018 disbursements; it is a debt account, not a $15 billion investment-stock inventory for the port and hinterland. Counting both the financing and the financed project as separate investment would double count. The original estimator's project list, valuation period and geographic boundary remain missing.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** The estimator's complete project-level reconciliation, distinguishing investment stock, contracts, commitments and disbursements.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** The report describes $15 billion as an estimate for the port and hinterlands. The IMF’s external-sector report instead lists individual projects by commencement year, including $530 million for the multipurpose port. Its table is not a cumulative sum of all Chinese commitments. A defensible reconciliation needs a defined period and a project ledger that distinguishes equity, debt, construction contracts and disbursements. This extends the estimate check in CMR06-R04. Consistency review, November 14, 2026. CMR06-R14 now has a port authority project figure of $590 million. It helps anchor one component and does not establish a $15 billion programme total. The comparison with CMR06-R04 should use the same geography and avoid double-counting construction and the financing that paid for it. Follow-up review, November 14, 2026. CMR06-R14 can now corroborate one $590 million project and Exim participation. That transaction covers a wider financing package and cannot be added to project investment as if it were a separate project. A complete project ledger and the estimate’s geographic scope remain needed. Follow-up review, November 15, 2026. The debt sustainability and corridor reports cover different subsets of activity. Neither provides a $15 billion stock of China-origin investment in the port and hinterland. The estimate requires a defined geography, a project list and a common valuation convention.
evidence: Djibouti Ports and Free Zones Authority, multipurpose port investment
IMF, Djibouti 2019 debt-sustainability analysis, loan and disbursement scope

rows.source: Djibouti population and capital-city share: vintage and denominator
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMR06-N131: The population is estimated below one million, with about 75 percent in the capital.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The current WDI historical population series is a revised vintage, whereas the chapter’s estimate was accessed in 2020. The Official Journal’s 2009 census is a separate benchmark with its own capital boundary and nonresident/population categories. Neither independently reconstructs the reported 2018 under-one-million estimate and 75% city share. National population and city proportion need a common vintage and boundary.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** The archived 2020 estimate and a defined capital-area numerator for the same year.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Reviewed November 11, 2026. The cited country landing page lacks a dated capital-city series in the extracted citation. The contemporaneous World Bank diagnostic instead describes the capital’s share as about 80 percent in Appendix 3. A specific historical population vintage and city boundary are needed to reconcile the estimates; current revised population figures should not be substituted silently for what was available in March 2020. Consistency review, November 14, 2026. The 2009 census decree gives 818,159 in the country and 475,322 in Djibouti ville, or about 58.1% under its census definition. The later World Bank diagnostic cites a higher share for the capital. The source years and geographic definitions differ. Use the dated census for its own comparison and leave the 75% historical estimate open. Follow-up review, November 14, 2026. The 2009 census and the World Bank diagnostic describe different dates and may use different city boundaries or population categories. The census figure refers to Djibouti ville. The March 2020 snapshot remains necessary for the country total and its intended capital-area denominator. Follow-up review, November 15, 2026. The World Bank’s contemporary estimate of about 80% refers to residence in the capital. An administrative-boundary or metro-area definition and the relevant population vintage could explain the difference from 75%. Neither is specified in the original citation. Source recheck. The current World Development Indicators historical population series returns 1,071,882 for 2018, above one million. Treat that as a revised comparator, not the value visible in March 2020. The capital-share figure remains dependent on the original vintage and city boundary. Neither can be reconstructed from the national denominator alone.
evidence: World Bank Djibouti diagnostic, Appendix 3, enterprise-survey coverage paragraph
St. Louis Fed mirror of World Bank national population data

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** Intervening official statements and the precise comparison between the earlier wording and the Djibouti facility’s publicly defined status.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Reviewed November 12, 2026. The October 2000 white paper says China did not station troops or establish military bases in foreign countries. This supports a specific earlier public position. Establishing continuity over many decades and determining the precise policy change requires additional official statements across the intervening years.

rows.source: Djibouti’s Chinese creditor exposure and the broader partner ranking
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMR06-N026. The report calls China Djibouti’s principal economic partner and creditor.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The recovered IMF debt discussions identify Chinese Eximbank as a major creditor, but a later arrears share measures neither total debt at the paper’s date nor overall economic partnership. Trade, investment and creditor exposure are separate rankings. The 2019 PDF was blocked and the old CGD link returned 404; the accessible later comparator cannot backdate the broader superlative.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** A contemporaneous creditor-stock table and an explicit trade/investment measure for the wider principal-partner claim.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Reviewed November 13, 2026. The cited IMF report’s debt sustainability analysis identifies three loans from China Exim Bank and says they accounted for about 71% of disbursements during 2014–18. That supports Chinese dominance in new public infrastructure financing in that period. A broader principal-economic-partner ranking requires comparable trade, investment and debt-stock measures for other partners. The original risk-tolerance wording is an inference. Rechecked November 14, 2026. The 2024 IMF debt analysis expressly calls China Exim the main creditor, confirming a later creditor ranking. That strengthens the creditor portion of the account. A claim of principal economic partner as of the paper’s date still requires a measure and contemporaneous comparison. Follow-up review, November 14, 2026. The IMF’s creditor evidence establishes a defined and narrower claim. Comparing trade, creditor stocks and investment is necessary before calling any economy the principal economic partner overall. Keep the earlier 71% figure tied to disbursements, rather than treating it as a share of all debt.
evidence: IMF Country Report 19/314, debt sustainability analysis paragraph 5
Center for Global Development policy paper 121, cited

rows.source: Which traffic the 90 percent Ethiopia–Djibouti estimate measures
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMR06-N103. The report attributes around 90% of all Djibouti port activity to Ethiopian trade.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The World Bank’s later Djibouti climate/development report distinguishes an 87% share of cargo in Djibouti’s ports attributable to Ethiopia from Djibouti’s approximately 95% share of Ethiopian international trade. Those inverse denominators cannot be substituted. The first corroborates the order of magnitude of the chapter’s 90%, but the original 2019 measure and its units remain unrecovered.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** The cited historical source, reporting year, port coverage and cargo measure; avoid reversing the trade denominator.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Reviewed November 13, 2026. The cited MOFCOM address now serves the 2025 edition, so its 2019 p. 25 could not be checked. UNCTAD and the World Bank report that more than 90% of Ethiopia’s foreign trade passes via Djibouti. That is a share of Ethiopia’s trade. To verify the report’s reverse ratio, obtain a same-year Djibouti port table of Ethiopian transit cargo and total cargo using the same volume units. Rechecked November 14, 2026. A World Bank transport study gives the reverse ratio directly at 85% of Djibouti port traffic in an earlier period. The Djibouti central bank’s 2022 report separately tabulates Ethiopian transit categories across 2018–22. These narrow the missing evidence, but the 2019 MOFCOM page and a matched same-year denominator for the study’s 90% remain unconfirmed. Follow-up review, November 15, 2026. The corridor appraisal uses Ethiopia’s trade as the denominator. The paper reverses that denominator. A matching Djibouti port report would need to identify both Ethiopian transit cargo and all port cargo in the same year and units. Source recheck. The World Bank’s Djibouti climate and development report independently estimates that 87% of the cargo handled in Djibouti’s ports is in transit or re-exported to Ethiopia. It separately reports Djibouti’s approximately 95% share of Ethiopia’s international trade. The first measure has the denominator intended by the paper and corroborates the order of magnitude. The original 2019 estimate and its year and units still need the cited source.
evidence: MOFCOM Ethiopia investment guide, replaced at original address
UNCTAD Ethiopia Diagnostic Trade Integration Study
World Bank Ethiopia Damage and Needs Assessment, Figure 6.2
World Bank transport and logistics study, Table 1
Djibouti central bank annual report 2022, Table 7, reproduced

rows.source: Doraleh’s 2018 container throughput needs a terminal-level series
rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR-06, PDF p. 13, performance paragraph, notes 62–63. The report gives 49,000 TEU against design capacity of 220,000 TEU for the multipurpose terminal.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The operator’s profile gives 200,000-TEU design capacity and prospective wording around 50,000 TEU in 2018. The actual 2018 annual report’s 7.5% decline refers to Port de Djibouti S.A.’s 0.86-million-TEU aggregate (PDF p. 22), not an independently identified 49,000-TEU DMP subtotal. A separate port presentation uses yet another capacity figure. Retain the terminal-level gap and avoid applying the company aggregate’s percentage to the small terminal.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** The original DMP 2018 tally and dated capacity specification; reconcile the adjacent aggregate-decline attribution.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** The source identified as the 2018 annual report was unavailable in full during this check. CMPort’s next interim report gives Port de Djibouti S.A. aggregate container throughput, with a different period and entity scope. For the cited utilization ratio, seek the 2018 multipurpose-terminal numerator and corresponding design capacity in TEU. Source recheck. A presentation specific to the multipurpose terminal supplies a distinct terminal-level source to compare with CMPort’s parent-company reporting. The report’s 2018 utilization fraction still requires an observed 2018 container total and a same-terminal container-capacity figure using the same unit. A presentation on the terminal cannot by itself authenticate the cited annual volumes. Source recheck. The operator’s terminal-specific page gives design capacity as 200,000 TEU and describes a 2018 figure of 50,000 TEU in prospective wording. The paper gives 220,000 design and 49,000 handled. The operator page supplies a close but distinct comparison at the correct terminal. The original 2018 terminal tally and dated capacity specification are still needed.

rows.source: The Ethiopia–Djibouti rail freight figure is a capacity claim
rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR-06, PDF p. 20, opening railway paragraph, note 105. The report cites capacity for 8.5 million tonnes of freight per year.
rows.finding: The cited Xinhua account was identified and the World Bank’s corridor appraisal documents the railway’s role in regional freight. The exact 8.5 million tonnes needs a dated railway design or operating document. Actual shipments for a given year would be a separate series. Source recheck. A dated Ethiopian Embassy account reports 8.5 million tonnes of freight per year as expected carrying volume for the new railway. The historical paper’s figure is supported as a project-era capacity projection. A 2024 commerce-ministry account separately reports measured freight figures, which should be kept distinct from that projection.

Chinese Commerce Ministry office, reported throughput

rows.source: Ethiopia’s reported agreement for a Djibouti port stake needs a closing record
rows.usage: Paraphrase of original passage. CMR-06, PDF p. 24, port investment paragraph, note 140. The report says Ethiopia agreed in 2018 to take a stake in the Port of Djibouti.
rows.finding: The cited Reuters dispatch attributes an agreement in principle to Ethiopian state media. That establishes the reported announcement. It provides neither a stake size nor proof of closing. A signed instrument or dated share register would establish whether the equity actually transferred. Source recheck. An official May 2, 2018 Ethiopian Embassy release records agreement to Ethiopia’s proposal and quotes the government spokesperson saying the percentage remained to be determined. This supports the paper’s claim that the governments reached an agreement in principle. The same evidence leaves the size and completion of any stake transfer open.
