rows.source: Libya projects: contract value is not measured loss
rows.usage: Note 21 says fifty Chinese projects halted in Libya resulted in an aggregate loss of nearly $20 billion.
rows.finding: A contemporary Xinhua account reproduced by the Chinese embassy states that 50 cooperative projects worth $18.8 billion were suspended. It identifies project value, not a measured financial loss of that amount. Revise the wording to suspended projects worth approximately $18.8 billion unless a separate loss assessment is supplied. The original Chen Chundi article still needs comparison to establish whether the distinction arose in that article or the citing study.
evidence: Contemporary Xinhua account reproduced by Chinese embassy

rows.source: Xianghuamen: owner name versus operator
rows.usage: The note is attached to: “Xianghuamen is owned and operated by the Nanjing Ocean Shipping Company.”
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The two China Daily incident URLs returned 404 in this check. The report’s ownership and operation assertion contains separate legal/commercial roles; a named shipowner in an incident story would not necessarily verify the operator or technical manager. A later sale or auction record also cannot establish all roles as of the 2012 incident.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** A dated registry or equivalent contemporaneous owner/operator/manager record for Xianghuamen.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Contemporary Xinhua reporting identifies Nanjing Ocean Shipping as the vessel’s owner, corroborating the ownership portion. The apparent difference between Ocean Shipping and Yuanyang may reflect translation of 远洋 rather than a different company. The checked account does not separately identify the ship manager or operator. Obtain the cited CCTV report or a contemporaneous registry record before certifying owned and operated as a combined assertion. Consistency review, November 14, 2026. Both older links support the event and identify the owner. Use the full legal name and date. A registry or equivalent source would be required to distinguish owning, operating and managing the same vessel, as in the fleet-perimeter check in CS21P2-R10. Follow-up review, November 14, 2026. The available dated incident reporting establishes the named owner. Owned and operated is a compound assertion and the source needs a registry manager or operator field from 2012 to support the second half. Do not use a later auction document as proof of the contemporaneous operator.

claim_review.original_source: Xianghuamen: owner name versus operator
claim_review.original_usage: The note is attached to: “Xianghuamen is owned and operated by the Nanjing Ocean Shipping Company.”
claim_review.remaining_gap: A dated registry or equivalent contemporaneous owner/operator/manager record for Xianghuamen.

rows.source: Full City: Chinese connection versus flag state
rows.usage: Note 130 describes the cargo ship attacked in May 2011 as Chinese-flagged.
rows.finding: The IMO’s May 2011 incident circular lists Full City, IMO 9073672, under Panama for the May 5 incident. Contemporary reporting also describes a Panama-flagged vessel with Chinese crew. Replace Chinese-flagged with Panama-flagged, Chinese-owned or Chinese-crewed as supported by the chosen source. paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CMS-10 — No Substitute for Experience: Chinese Antipiracy Operations in the Gulf of Aden (Andrew S. Erickson & Austin M. Strange, November 2013)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: China Maritime Study No. 10 is the most detailed open-source account of the PLAN's Gulf of Aden deployments, drawing on more than two thousand Chinese-language sources. Erickson and Strange argue that antipiracy offered Beijing a politically safe, internationally welcome way to begin regularized far-seas operations, and that the experience gained — in logistics, long-duration voyages, coordination with civilian agencies, and engagement with other navies — is raising PLAN capability and confidence for future nontraditional and, by extension, other far-seas missions, though the PLA remains ground-force dominated.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Authors' Note and Introduction (pp. 1–20)**: Sources, port-call table, why antipiracy.
• **Chapter 1: Modern Piracy and Its Relevance to China (pp. 21–56)**: Shipping dependence, 2008 incidents, public and political pressure.
• **Chapter 2: Institutional Underpinnings (pp. 57–68)**: Domestic drivers and policy processes.
• **Chapter 3: China's Views on Multilateral Coordination (pp. 69–93)**: Groups, independent forces, law.
• **Chapter 4: Operations (pp. 94–132)**: Platforms, logistics, escort procedures, encounters.
• **Chapter 5: Operational Trajectories (pp. 133–178)**: Logistics trends, platforms, carriers, basing, best practices.
• **Experience and Future Missions (pp. 179–198)** and **Conclusion (pp. 199–201)**; **Appendix: Notional PLAN Order of Battle (p. 202)**.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Concepts**: *escort task force* (护航编队), *transport dadui*-style civil coordination with the Ministry of Transport, *far seas* operations, *nontraditional security*, *public goods*, *piracy versus 'hijacking'* in Chinese usage.
• **Quantitative claims**: `15` task forces, December 2008 to 2013; first TF `Wuhan`, `Haikou`, `Weishanhu` (26 December 2008); `83` of `1,265` Chinese ships attacked in 2008; `86%` of netizens in favor; MoT: `3,300+` vessels, `84.88` Mt, `4th`, `90%` of trade by sea, `40,000` crewmen; `2,000+` Chinese sources; port-call table `14` task forces, February 2009–April 2013.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 7 reference rows audited in `CMS-10`, 4 are rated `ok` and 3 are rated `unk`; no `fix` was found:
• **`[CMS10-R02]` (`unk` — Shipping Statistics)**: The '40,000 crewmen' figure is not reconcilable with later mariner counts.
• **`[CMS10-R06]` (`unk` — Institutional Effects)**: The authors' inference about organizational impact.
• **`[CMS10-R07]` (`unk` — Appendix Order of Battle)**: The table was not readable.

The study is the **definitive English-language account of PLAN antipiracy operations** and the best baseline for later work on far-seas deployment, escort practice and basing (`CMR-06`, `CMS-13`, `CMR-08`). Its main limits are its date (2013), the garbled appendix and its reliance on Chinese official media for operational details.

**Footnote rows**: all 921 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 591 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMS10-S4N001 to CMS10-S13N084). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 921 notes: 136 (15%) are confirmed, 8 of them against a retrieved source and 128 after an outside web search (82 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 30 are flagged for reader check; 785 (85%) are not confirmed. Of the 785 notes not confirmed, 416 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 74 were judged not web-checkable (1 note that is a fragment or run-on text attached to a Chinese-language source; 6 the authors' own data, imagery or analysis; 22 private interviews or conversations; 8 print-only books or paywalled items; 9 notes that are explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation; 28 other items); 295 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 591 source rows are 89 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 502 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMS10-S4N003`: The sentence says the PLA Navy deployed nearly ten thousand personnel on thirty-seven warships with twenty-eight helicopters in thirteen task forces over four years; `CMS10-S5N001`: The sentence says, citing a Zhongxing News report on EU naval officers, that the number of pirate attacks rose threefold in 2010. The only "threefold" found is an EU NAVFOR comparison of pirate groups disrupted in a 12-week period against the year before; `CMS10-S5N041`: The sentence gives $2.2 million to the African Union and $780,000 to Burundi and Uganda. The $2.2 million is confirmed; no source found gives $780,000, and other sources describe different aid to Uganda (about $2.7 million, or 17 million yuan); and 27 more. 119 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CMS-11 — China's Near Seas Combat Capabilities (Peter Dutton, Andrew S. Erickson & Ryan Martinson, eds., February 2014)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: China Maritime Study No. 11 brings together eight analyses of the PLA's capabilities in the near seas — the area out to the First Island Chain and about 500 nautical miles. The chapters on Houbei fast attack craft, submarines and ASW, the Second Artillery, aerospace power, air superiority, C4ISR, space-based ISR and the surface fleet argue that these capabilities are advancing together to support a counterstrike strategy against U.S. and allied forces in China's near seas, with the PLAN's surface fleet on a path toward fleets for Taiwan, East Asia and global operations.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Chapter 1 (Patch)**: Houbei fast attack craft beyond sea denial.
• **Chapter 2 (Murray)**: Underwater TELs and China's ASW.
• **Chapter 3 (Christman)**: The Second Artillery Force.
• **Chapter 4 (Kostecka)**: Aerospace power and counterstrike doctrine.
• **Chapter 5 (Shlapak)**: Air superiority and stealth aircraft.
• **Chapter 6 (Pedersen)**: Land- and sea-based C4ISR.
• **Chapter 7 (Erickson)**: Air- and space-based ISR.
• **Chapter 8 (Walton and McGrath)**: Surface fleet trajectory and the three fleets.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Concepts**: *near seas* (the First Island Chain out to ~500 nm), *near-seas active defense*, *counterstrike* (反击), *sea denial versus sea control*, *Houbei*, *rationally weak ASW*, *fused picture*, *three fleets*.
• **Quantitative claims**: Type 022 `>60` (ch. 1), `80` (press), `60` (DoD 2012), `83` (ch. 8 table); missile boats `175` (`83` + `92`); amphibious ships `56`; mine warfare vessels `27`; subchasers `75`; carriers `1`; hospital ships `6`; J-20 first flight `January 2011`; Tianlian-1-03 launch `25 July 2012`.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 6 reference rows audited in `CMS-11`, 2 are rated `ok` and 4 are rated `unk`; no `fix` was found:
• **`[CMS11-R01]` (`unk` — Houbei Count)**: The volume gives sixty, eighty and 83 for the same force.
• **`[CMS11-R03]`, `[CMS11-R04]`, `[CMS11-R06]` (`unk`)**: Scenario analyses, capability projections and fleet-trajectory forecasts that could not be tested.

The volume is the **most compact multi-author survey of PLA near-seas combat capabilities circa 2013** and a baseline against which later developments can be measured (`CMR-05`, `CMSI-T31`, `CMSI-T32`, `CNN-07`). Its limits are its date, the partly unreadable tables and the fact that most conclusions are scenario-based assessments.

**Footnote rows**: all 411 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 305 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMS11-S1N001 to CMS11-S12N027). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 411 notes: 139 (34%) are confirmed, 3 of them against a retrieved source and 136 after an outside web search (107 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 22 are flagged for reader check; 272 (66%) are not confirmed. Of the 272 notes not confirmed, 47 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 38 were judged not web-checkable (6 the authors' own data, imagery or analysis; 13 print-only books or paywalled items; 17 notes that are explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation; 2 other items); 187 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 305 source rows are 99 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 206 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMS11-S1N025`: The sentences give the YJ-83 (C-803) range as 135 nautical miles in one place and 160 nautical miles in Jane's World Navies in another. Sources found give 180 km (about 97 nm) for the YJ-83 and C-802A, 230 km for a later variant, and GlobalSecurity cites about 135 nm (250 km); no source gave 160 nm; `CMS11-S1N030`: The sentences give the YJ-83 (C-803) range as 135 nautical miles in one place and 160 nautical miles in Jane's World Navies in another. Sources found give 180 km (about 97 nm) for the YJ-83 and C-802A, 230 km for a later variant, and GlobalSecurity cites about 135 nm (250 km); no source gave 160 nm; `CMS11-S1N046`: The sentence says (citing Cordesman and Hammond) that Taiwan has sixty-one fast attack guided-missile craft, of which eighteen Kuang-Hua VIs with four Hsiung Feng-2 missiles make up the modern force; and 19 more. 87 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

sections.heading: Open claim-audit follow-up, November 22, 2026 (review complete; gaps recorded)
sections.body:
This continuation targets 8 initially open claim audits in this paper. 8 have a recorded individual follow-up: 2 now have a supported or correction finding; 6 remain unresolved. 0 of this paper’s initial open audits still await this continuation. Every reviewed row retains its evidence limits; a completed follow-up does not mean every substantive claim is verified.

[CMS11-R08](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-11&row=CMS11-R08): Correction established. No remaining gap for the mismatch between the cited wording and the narrower paraphrase; any separate 2050 informatization-completion claim needs its own source.

[CMS11-R01](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-11&row=CMS11-R01): Reviewed; unresolved. Source dates and operational/commissioned/in-construction definitions for each quoted count, plus a common-date hull list.

[CMS11-R03](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-11&row=CMS11-R03): Reviewed; unresolved. Original dated sources for the separate equipment and inventory assertions; independently substantiated evidence for the inferred organizational choice and hypothetical outcomes.

[CMS11-R04](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-11&row=CMS11-R04): Reviewed; unresolved. Original dated first-flight and role records for the factual components; independent performance evidence for the much stronger comparison.

[CMS11-R06](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-11&row=CMS11-R06): Reviewed; unresolved. A stated forecast-evaluation rule and dated comparison evidence for the distinct capability assertions.

[CMS11-R07](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-11&row=CMS11-R07): Reviewed; unresolved. The original agency imagery inventory, date/time coverage, quality criteria and task-specific use record.

[CMS11-R10](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-11&row=CMS11-R10): Reviewed; unresolved. Independent dated historical evidence for the trend and precise scope, without treating policy statements as performance measurements.

[CMS11-R11](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-11&row=CMS11-R11): Correction established. Observed coordination and any narrower claim about newly assigned 2010 functions need separate evidence.

paper_memo.memo_title: Audit Memo: The Recruitment, Education, and Training of PLA Navy Personnel (Allen & Clemens, 2014)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: China Maritime Study No. 12 is a compact, source-heavy account of how the PLA Navy recruits, educates and trains its officers and enlisted personnel. Its thesis is that the PLAN's personnel system basically mirrors the PLA's, that the Navy has tried since the 1990s to raise the educational level of its force by using the civilian university system (National Defense Students for officers, direct recruitment of graduates and vocational-college students as NCOs), and that the reforms are only partly implemented and will take decades to mature.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Introduction**: Liu Huaqing's 'capable personnel' remark; the 1999 conscript-NCO reform, the mid-2000s direct NCO recruitment, the 2009 shift and problems by 2011; women in the PLAN.
• **Officer recruitment and education**: Seven academic institutions, the National Defense Student Program, graduate-school options and the probationary first year.
• **Professional military education**: The surface-branch career track and continuing education tied to grade promotion.
• **Unit-level training**: Training inside operational units.
• **Enlisted recruitment and basic training**: Two-year conscripts, new-soldier training at fleet bases.
• **NCO training and education**: The direct-recruitment pilot program, NCO schools, specialty training and the skills-evaluation system.
• **Conclusions**: Aspirational PME, continued emphasis on skills training, reliance on civilian education.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Concepts**: *National Defense Student (国防生) Program*, *Reserve Officer (后备军官) Program*, *noncommissioned officer (士官) corps*, *direct recruitment (直接招收)*, *professional military education (PME)*, *probationary (见习) year*, *vocational skills evaluation (职业技能鉴定)*.
• **Quantitative claims**: NDS goal `60%` (April 2007) versus `40%` (Conclusions) by 2010; `~100,000` officer graduates/year (`70/30`, December 2009); `118` universities (`13` for PLAN); NDS female cap `15%`; SSF `300` NDS officers, `86` (`29%`) with master's; NCO service up to `30` years; Zhenghe `9` and `13` female cadets, `110` cadets (2012); pilot NCO program `390` versus `830` students; SSF base `3,000` new soldiers (2011–12).

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 7 reference rows audited in `CMS-12`, 2 are rated `ok`, 4 are rated `unk` and 1 is rated `fix`:
• **`[CMS12-R01]` (`fix` — NDS Goal)**: The body gives a 60 percent target for 2010; the Conclusions give 40 percent.
• **`[CMS12-R02]`, `[CMS12-R04]`, `[CMS12-R06]`, `[CMS12-R07]` (`unk`)**: Claims resting on Chinese-language articles that could not be retrieved, or that the authors themselves flag as conflicting.

The monograph is the **most detailed English-language account of PLAN personnel pipelines circa 2013**, useful for tracing how the Navy's officer and NCO corps were meant to change (`CMS-11`, `CMR-05`). Its limits are its date (before the 2015–16 reorganization) and its dependence on Chinese web sources that were not independently verified.

**Footnote rows**: all 118 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 107 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMS12-N001 to CMS12-N118). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 118 notes: 4 (3%) are confirmed, 0 of them against a retrieved source and 4 after an outside web search (4 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 2 are flagged for reader check; 114 (97%) are not confirmed. Of the 114 notes not confirmed, 75 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 12 were judged not web-checkable (2 private interviews or conversations; 3 print-only books or paywalled items; 7 notes that are explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation); 27 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 107 source rows are 4 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 103 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMS12-N035`: The sentence says the figures come from a December 2009 Jiefangjun Bao article. The Jamestown account of the same 70/30 split dates the PLA Daily article to 30 November 2009; the original article was not retrieved and the Jamestown piece is by the monograph's author, so the date may be a slip in either text; `CMS12-N036`: The sentence says the PLA capped female national defense students at 15 percent (source: a Fujian Education Department entrance-exam page). Jamestown reports an initial 5 percent maximum applied inconsistently, and one 2015 university example gives 10 percent for undergraduates and 20 percent for graduates; the cap may have…. 24 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

sections.heading: Open claim-audit follow-up, November 22, 2026 (review complete; gaps recorded)
sections.body:
This continuation targets 8 initially open claim audits in this paper. 8 have a recorded individual follow-up: 0 now have a supported or correction finding; 8 remain unresolved. 0 of this paper’s initial open audits still await this continuation. Every reviewed row retains its evidence limits; a completed follow-up does not mean every substantive claim is verified.

[CMS12-R02](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-12&row=CMS12-R02): Reviewed; unresolved. Sun Zhi's exact original newspaper item and annual graduate definitions; a rule explicitly applying the female cap to National Defense Students.

[CMS12-R04](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-12&row=CMS12-R04): Reviewed; unresolved. The 2009 policy and intake data defining the college share and whether the assertion concerns recruits, NCOs or the whole enlisted force.

[CMS12-R06](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-12&row=CMS12-R06): Reviewed; unresolved. The original Renmin Haijun article and the Shandong report, with their dates, intake categories and complete institution lists.

[CMS12-R07](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-12&row=CMS12-R07): Reviewed; unresolved. The original service-paper passage or implementation order and a clear definition of the institutions included in the seven-unit count.

[CMS12-R08](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-12&row=CMS12-R08): Reviewed; unresolved. The original dated Sun Zhi item and an annual source defining the graduate population and the two routes.

[CMS12-R09](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-12&row=CMS12-R09): Reviewed; unresolved. A dated policy explicitly imposing the claimed 15-percent National Defense Student ceiling, rather than an academy rule or a provincial intake outcome.

[CMS12-R13](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-12&row=CMS12-R13): Reviewed; unresolved. A dated 2010 graduate-destination/cohort table and the original cited notice.

[CMS12-R14](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-12&row=CMS12-R14): Reviewed; unresolved. The original April notice and finalized agreement or subsequent university implementation report.

rows.source: Gulf of Aden Escort Totals at the Sixth Anniversary (End of 2014): Fifteen Thousand Personnel in Nineteen Task Forces, Nearly Six Thousand Merchant Ships (About Half Foreign) in Eight Hundred Batches; Eight Vessels Delivered after Release by Pirates, Eight Rescued under Attack, Forty-three Saved from the Chase of Pirates, Five Others Assisted (Chapter 4)
rows.usage: Quantifies the results of the PLAN's first six years of antipiracy operations.
rows.finding: Plausible and consistent with other reporting (about 5,000 ships escorted by end-2013, rising toward 6,000 a year later; 26 December 2008 start); the totals come from Chinese official statements and could not be independently counted. See `CMS13-R02` for a conflicting figure elsewhere in the volume.

rows.source: Zhang Junshe's August 2013 Totals: Fifteen Flotillas, Forty Warships, Thirty-two Helicopters, 'More Than Six Thousand' Merchant Ships Protected (Half Foreign), Four WFP Ships, Four Ships Recovered from Pirates, More Than Twenty Saved from Pursuit (Chapter 5)
rows.usage: Gives the Chinese naval view of the antipiracy mission's scale through mid-2013.
rows.finding: Internal conflict with Chapter 4 (`fix`): 'more than six thousand' ships by August 2013 cannot be reconciled with 'nearly six thousand' at the end of 2014 after four more task forces, and external reporting puts the total near 5,000 at end-2013; the fifteen flotillas of two warships plus a supply ship also give about thirty warships, not forty, unless repeat deployments are counted.

rows.source: Cautious Rules of Engagement and Cooperation: Taiankou (Nov. 2010, 21 Crewmen Sheltered in Citadel), Shiuh-fu (2012, Twelfth Task Force, Changzhou); 25 August 2013 Joint Exercise with USS Mason (DDG 87), Harbin (112) and Weishanhu; Joint U.S.–China Antipiracy Exercises in 2012, 2013 and 2014 (Chapters 4–5)
rows.usage: Illustrates the PLAN's limited use of force and its operational cooperation with the U.S. Navy.
rows.finding: Internally consistent; the August 2013 Mason–Harbin counterpiracy exercise matches contemporaneous U.S. and Chinese reporting, and the ship numbers (Haikou 171, Wuhan 169, Weishanhu 887, Harbin 112) are consistent. The Taiankou and Shiuh-fu details rest on Chinese-language media not retrieved here.

rows.source: Economic Basis for Overseas Basing: China–Africa Trade from US$10 Billion (2000) to US$127 Billion (2010); Chinese Direct Investment in Africa from US$490 Million (2003) to US$9.33 Billion (2009); 22 Percent of 2010 Outbound Investors in Africa; Expatriates from 3.5 Million (2005) to 5.5 Million (2011) (Chapter 6)
rows.usage: Supplies the economic and demographic reasons for China to consider overseas military access.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** Two substantial components are now settled. Ambassador Gong Jianzhong's March 2011 speech gives direct-investment amounts at the end of 2003 and end of 2009, identifying the $490 million/$9.33 billion comparison as a stock comparison. The 2013 white paper independently labels the 2009 $9.33 billion accumulated investment. Downs's actual April 13, 2011 testimony, p. 1, gives estimated Chinese workers abroad of 3.5 million in 2005 and 5.5 million today; it is a global worker estimate, not an Africa-only or all-residents census. The earlier trade source supports $126.9 billion in 2010. The separate 22-percent company share remains unverified; do not derive it by dividing differently dated enterprise totals.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** The original 2010 company-population denominator and MOFCOM passage behind the 22-percent figure; the underlying methodology of the attributed worker estimate remains distinct from verifying its quotation.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** The trade figures match widely reported totals (roughly US$10 billion to US$127 billion) and the 'more than tenfold' rise is correct arithmetic; the investment figures are not labeled as stock or flow and could not be tied to a MOFCOM table, and the expatriate estimates depend on a single Brookings estimate (`unk`). Follow-up review, November 15, 2026. The Commerce Ministry’s public briefing confirms $126.9 billion in bilateral trade for 2010, and the trade white paper distinguishes direct-investment flows and stock. The passage’s investment figures and population estimate still need their original series and coverage. Source recheck. The original NBER trade study gives $10.6 billion for all-Africa imports plus exports in 2000 and $7 billion for sub-Saharan Africa alone. This pins down the baseline’s geographic definition. It does not verify the accompanying overseas population figure or the distinction between investment stock and commitments.
evidence: State Council trade and economic cooperation white paper
Original NBER trade and investment study
Ambassador Gong Jianzhong, March 2011 speech, end-year investment stocks
Downs, original April 13, 2011 testimony, p. 1, global worker estimate
State Council, China-Africa Economic and Trade Cooperation (2013), accumulated investment comparison

rows.source: Six Overseas Basing Models and the Forecast: 'Pit Stop,' 'Lean Colonial' Network, 'Dual-Use Logistics Facility,' 'String of Pearls,' 'Warehouse,' 'Model USA'; Table 1 Criteria; Judgment that a Dual-Use Facility Using Local Agents Is Most Likely (Chapter 6)
rows.usage: Frames the options and predicts which overseas logistics arrangement the PLAN will adopt.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The chapter's conclusion on PDF p. 69 uses if-and-when and most-likely language for a dual-use logistics model, and describes a light footprint and local supply relationships. It is a forecast whose alternatives are analytical constructs. A later base can be evaluated against that forecast only with explicit criteria for footprint, functions and local-agent dependence. The existence of Djibouti alone cannot validate every feature of the earlier model. Keep the forecast attributed and its later assessment distinct from the contemporary observations.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** A defined comparison framework and dated evidence about the actual facilities if the six-model prediction is to be tested.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** A forecast built from Chinese commentary and the author's weighing of costs (`unk`): the chapter observes that China used Salalah, Aden, Djibouti and Karachi with no long-term basing agreement and three-to-five-ship deployments, but it cannot be tested from the volume; later events, including the Djibouti support base covered in CMR-06, should be compared against its 'small, light footprint' expectation.

claim_review.original_usage: Frames the options and predicts which overseas logistics arrangement the PLAN will adopt.

rows.source: China's Oil and Trade Dependence: 5.1 Million Barrels per Day of Crude Imported in 2011, 'Roughly 20 Percent' of Oil Consumption; About 40 Percent of Oil Imports through Hormuz; Seaborne Commerce 'Over 10 Percent' of GDP (Chapter 7) versus Foreign Trade at 47 Percent of GDP in 2012 with 80–90 Percent by Ship (Chapter 10) and 80 Percent by Value and 90 Percent by Weight (Chapter 9)
rows.usage: Quantifies China's dependence on seaborne trade and imported oil in the case for far-seas operations.
rows.finding: Internal conflict (`fix`): 5.1 million barrels per day imported is more than half of China's roughly 9–10 million barrels per day consumption in 2011, not 20 percent; and 47 percent of GDP × 80–90 percent carried by sea implies seaborne trade near 38–42 percent of GDP, far above 'over 10 percent.' The 47 percent of GDP figure itself matches World Bank data for 2012.

rows.source: U.S. Surveillance and Survey Incidents in China's EEZ: EP-3 Collision (1 April 2001), USNS Bowditch (March 2001, September 2002), Impeccable and Victorious (2009; Impeccable Surrounded on 9 March 2009 About Seventy-Five Miles South of Hainan), USS Cowpens (December 2013); MMCA Formalized 1998 (Chapter 10; Chapter 8 notes)
rows.usage: Establishes the record of friction over foreign military activities in China's EEZ.
rows.finding: Dates and platforms match the well-known record; 1 April 2001 EP-3 collision, 9 March 2009 Impeccable harassment, December 2013 Cowpens encounter and 1998 MMCA are all consistent with other sources. The chapter's description of all incidents as 'aggressive maneuvers' meant to deter surveillance is the authors' characterization rather than a Chinese admission.

rows.source: Odom's Argument that China's Restrictive Law-of-the-Sea Position Could Hamper Far-Seas Missions, Wang Xiaoxuan's 'Eliminate Exclusive Control of the Straits' and the Editors' Rules-versus-Relationships Contrast (Chapters 8–9; Introduction)
rows.usage: Frames the legal and conceptual difference between U.S. and Chinese approaches to EEZ military activities and sea-lane security.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The editor's rules-versus-relationships contrast appears on PDF p. 14 as a recurring theme in this volume and discussions, rather than a measured national disposition. Odom's legal-policy reasoning and Wang's preferred arrangements likewise remain attributed arguments. The evidence does not turn a recommended legal interpretation into an authoritative PRC policy or establish that one national approach uniformly dominates. Independent wording checks and a transparent comparison sample would be necessary for the broader generalization.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** Original attributed passages where translation is at issue, and an explicit comparison sample for the national approaches generalization.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** These are positional arguments rather than checkable facts (`unk`): Odom's claim that a liberal reading of military freedoms would best serve China, Wang's call for joint management and the editors' summary that Americans prefer rules and Chinese prefer relationships cannot be verified against the text alone, and Wang makes little reference to the legal regime.

rows.source: Date of Gates’s quoted Shangri-La Dialogue remarks
rows.usage: The note is attached to: “In a speech at the Shangri-La Dialogue in June 2010, then–Secretary of Defense Robert Gates highlighted the importance of this precept with an interesting choice of words—a “just international order that emphasizes rights and responsibilities of nations and fidelity to the rule of law.””
rows.finding: The quoted phrase is in the Defense Department transcript of Gates’s 4 June 2011 address to the tenth Shangri-La Dialogue. The 2010 remarks are a separate speech. Cite the 2011 address for this wording.
evidence: Defense Department transcript as reproduced by VOA

rows.source: Late-1970 Soviet agreement to discuss incidents at sea
rows.usage: The grouped row’s note 18 places Soviet agreement to discussions in late 1970.
rows.finding: The National Defense University’s historical account explicitly says the Soviets relented in late 1970. Agreement to negotiate is distinct from the later meetings and the signed 1972 accord. The paper’s date is supported for the acceptance milestone.
evidence: NDU, Managing Sino-U.S. Air and Naval Interactions, p. 12

rows.source: Military maritime freedoms: historical commentary and pinpoint citation
rows.usage: Note 29 cites p. 16 of the 1994 presidential treaty-transmittal package for military intelligence collection and surveillance among maritime freedoms.
rows.finding: Later U.S. Senate committee language expressly includes intelligence collection and surveillance among the U.S. understanding of internationally lawful military uses. It corroborates that U.S. position but does not establish the content of p. 16 in the 1994 package. Congress.gov confirms the treaty’s identity and date but says pre-1995 treaty-document full texts are unavailable there. Obtain the 1994 commentary and distinguish it from the short presidential letter; do not label the citation wrong solely because the letter itself is short. Consistency review, November 14, 2026. The Senate Foreign Relations Committee hosts the complete 1994 transmittal package. Its Article 87 commentary includes surveillance and intelligence gathering among uses under the U.S. interpretation. This directly supports the attribution. Distinguish the commentary from treaty wording, as in CAPP2-R06.
evidence: Congress.gov treaty document and historical-text availability
U.S. Senate Treaty Document 103-39, Article 87 commentary

rows.source: Eyes-in-the-Sky: launch predates Thailand’s full membership
rows.usage: The note is attached to: “Thailand’s later joining in this initiative led to “eyes in the sky” patrols to enhance coordinated aerial surveillance of the straits.”
rows.finding: Singapore’s May 2009 ministerial speech dates the air-patrol initiative to September 2005 and Thailand’s joining the broader patrol framework to September 2008. The official fact sheet likewise places air patrols in 2005. Revise the causal chronology so Thailand’s later membership is not described as leading to the earlier launch; distinguish launch participation from later full membership.
evidence: Official Malacca Straits Patrol fact sheet

rows.source: Japan counterpiracy command: announcement and assumption dates
rows.usage: The note is attached to: “Already likely to continue contributions, on the strength of policies and past practice, the PLAN became almost certain to do so following the announcement in late 2014 that the navy of China’s East Asian rival Japan, the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force, would soon take command of a major international antipiracy coalition.”
rows.finding: The footnote itself dates the Kyodo report July 18, 2014, whereas the passage says late 2014. Combined Maritime Forces records Japan’s first CTF 151 command beginning May 31, 2015. These are announcement and assumption milestones, not competing dates for one event. Retrieve the Kyodo text to fix the announcement wording. Neither milestone alone establishes the author’s prediction that China was almost certain to continue contributing. Follow-up review, November 15, 2026. An announcement reported in July and assumption of command the following May are separate events. The source trail raises a correction to ‘late 2014’, while the author's prediction about motives cannot be established from the timing of the appointments. Source recheck. The UK Foreign Secretary publicly welcomed the planned Japanese command on July 28, 2014. The decision was therefore public by July, so the late-2014 wording should be corrected. The first assumption of command already documented for May 2015 is a separate event. The exact July announcement day and the paper’s forecast of Chinese policy remain separate questions.

rows.source: China’s seaborne trade share: historical measure
rows.usage: The note is attached to: “Some 80–90 percent of this trade is carried by ship.”
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The original NBS statistical release distinguishes merchandise trade valued in dollars from port foreign-trade cargo measured in tonnes. Port throughput includes its own counting rules and does not supply a modal share for all trade. APEC’s fleet-carriage measures are also different. These sources cannot authenticate the study’s 80–90% without its historical denominator and scope.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** A matched historical all-mode trade dataset and explicit volume/value definition for the stated range.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** The cited April 2009 article is identifiable in Xinhua’s archive, but its full text and Cole’s relevant page were not retrieved. The 80–90 percent share remains unverified for its historical year and denominator. Later percentages measured by cargo volume cannot establish the earlier proportion of trade by value. Retain uncertainty until the original source specifies the measure. Consistency review, November 14, 2026. Cross-check CMS09-R07's 85% and CMS10-R02's 90% separately. APEC's report distinguishes national carriage, and later figures measured in freight tonnes cannot backfill an earlier claim about trade value. The sentence still needs the historical source's unit. Follow-up review, November 14, 2026. The original note cites an April 2009 article and a 2010 edition of Cole separately from port rankings. Keep the 80–90% historical trade share apart from port throughput and a recent freight-volume percentage. The exact sentence and metric in those older sources remain needed. Follow-up review, November 15, 2026. The contemporary Xinhua archive establishes the title and publication context of one reference. The original wording or Cole’s page is needed to identify whether the historical estimate measured trade value, tonnes or a share of cargo categories. Source recheck. The 2005 NBS communiqué reports foreign-trade cargo throughput in tonnes and merchandise trade separately in U.S. dollars. This fixes the quantities available in that contemporary statistical release. Port throughput is not a modal share of total trade value or a complete series of all international freight modes, so the passage still needs the original historical denominator.
evidence: Xinhua historical index identifying the cited article
APEC cargo preference study, different national-fleet denominator
NBS 2005 communiqué, transport and external-economy tables

rows.source: Resolution 2184: renewal date and duration
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMS13-S4N003: The passage says the Security Council extended Somali counterpiracy authorization on November 12, 2014 until November 12, 2015.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 11, 2026. Confirmed: the resolution is dated November 12, 2014 and operative paragraph 13 renews the authorizations for twelve months from that date. Paragraph 14 retains the Somalia-specific and consent qualifications; this was not a general global counterpiracy mandate. Checked the official resolution PDF.

rows.source: Resolution 1801 and the count of six 2008 piracy resolutions
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMS13-S4N005: The passage identifies Resolution 1801 as one of six resolutions mentioning Somali piracy that year.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 11, 2026. Resolution 1801’s paragraph 12 expressly addresses piracy and protection of shipping, so that part is confirmed. The exact annual count is not established by this citation: official UN discussions also include Resolution 1814 in the 2008 counterpiracy sequence, while the study’s following notes enumerate other instruments. The word “mentioning” and the scope of the count need reconciliation against a complete annual set; no exact total is certified here. Rechecked November 14, 2026. The UN’s 2008 Juridical Yearbook gives a five-resolution subset. Resolution 1801 also mentions piracy and the Security Council repertory includes 1814 in the sequence. Present the enumerated set and its inclusion rule rather than a bare total of six for every resolution mentioning piracy.
evidence: UN Security Council Repertoire, 2008–2009, Resolution 1814 paragraph 11
UN Juridical Yearbook 2008, legal activities review
UN Division for Ocean Affairs piracy document index

rows.source: Resolution 1816: six-month territorial-waters authorization
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMS13-S4N006: The passage says Resolution 1816 initially permitted all necessary means against piracy in Somali territorial waters for six months.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 11, 2026. Confirmed in paragraph 7, subject to cooperation with the Transitional Federal Government and its advance notification to the Secretary-General. Paragraph 9 confines the authorization to Somalia and records the government’s consent. The six-month term is correct; omitting these conditions would overstate which States and activities were authorized. Checked the official resolution text.

rows.source: Resolutions 1838, 1844 and 1846: concern and Somali requests
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMS13-S4N007: The passage says Resolutions 1838 and 1844 expressed concern about piracy and Resolution 1846 recorded Somali requests for assistance and extension.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 11, 2026. Confirmed in scope. Resolution 1838 condemns piracy; Resolution 1844’s preamble expresses grave concern and links piracy with financing embargo violations. The UN’s operative-text registry for 1846 records renewal of the territorial-waters authorization; the later official 1851 preamble records Somali requests and appreciation. The direct 1846 PDF was unavailable, so its precise preambular wording was not certified from that PDF. This check concerns the documented authorization sequence, not a new general right of intervention. Rechecked November 14, 2026. The recovered 1846 text expressly welcomes the Somali request conveyed on November 20, 2008 and records Somali consent. This closes the earlier gap in the wording and supports the chapter’s characterization alongside 1838 and 1844.
evidence: UN Security Council Resolution 1846, preamble and paragraph 11

rows.source: Resolution 1851: in-Somalia measures and the December 2 clock
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMS13-S4N008: The passage says Resolution 1851 authorized measures in Somalia for twelve months beginning December 2, 2008.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 11, 2026. Paragraph 6 confirms a twelve-month term from adoption of Resolution 1846, rather than from 1851’s own December 16 adoption. It authorizes appropriate measures in Somalia pursuant to the Somali government’s request and advance notification, with humanitarian and human-rights-law conditions. This supports the passage’s broader geographic point but preserves the conditions absent from its short summary. Checked the official PDF.

rows.source: The 2009–2013 twelve-month renewal sequence
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMS13-S4N009: The note lists Resolutions 1897, 1950, 2020, 2077 and 2125 as successive twelve-month renewals.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 11, 2026. The UN’s text of Resolution 2125 paragraph 12 identifies the earlier renewal provisions; the official Resolution 2184 paragraph 13 repeats that chain and the 2013 renewal. These primary cross-references support the sequence and annual duration. The five original PDFs were not each independently opened, and no claim about uninterrupted operational participation by a particular navy is inferred.

rows.source: The 2011 LNG share and its geographic referent
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMS13-S3N005: The extracted sentence says roughly half of world LNG trade passed through “it” in 2011.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 11, 2026. The April 4, 2013 EIA article reports more than half of global LNG trade, about 6 trillion cubic feet, passing through the South China Sea in 2011. This resolves the missing source item but not the extracted pronoun’s referent. It does not establish the same percentage specifically for the Strait of Malacca. The surrounding original passage could not be retrieved, so geographic equivalence remains unchecked and the sentence is not marked fully verified. Consistency review, November 14, 2026. The EIA source explicitly assigns the 2011 figure of more than half to the South China Sea. Its separate passage discusses additional future supply moving through Malacca. Align geography with CESP4-R09 and require the preceding sentence of this chapter to resolve its pronoun. Follow-up review, November 14, 2026. The original CMS-13 extract’s sentence immediately before roughly half names the Strait of Malacca. The cited EIA article’s 2011 figure is for the South China Sea. Correct the geography in the claim or cite separate transit data for Malacca.
evidence: EIA Today in Energy, April 4, 2013, LNG paragraph
EIA, April 4, 2013, explicit 2011 regional LNG figure

rows.source: Xi’s June 8, 2013 quotation: extra wording in the English extract
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMS13-S7N005: The quotation inserts nonconflict and nonconfrontation into the sentence describing a new model of major-country relations.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 11, 2026. The cited White House English transcript’s sentence lists mutual respect and win-win cooperation; it does not contain the two added terms there. The preceding sentence discusses avoiding confrontation and conflict, so the general idea is consistent, but the displayed quotation is not verbatim. Use an explicit paraphrase or the transcript’s wording. This checks the cited English version, not the original Chinese audio or an alternative translation.
evidence: White House transcript, June 8, 2013, Xi’s new-model paragraph

rows.source: China’s straight baselines and the scope of foreign-ship exclusion
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMS13-S8N004: China seeks straight baselines along its entire coastline, enclosing extensive waters off limits to foreign ships.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 11, 2026. The February 25, 1992 law defines internal waters landward of baselines (Article 2), prescribes straight baselines and a 12-nautical-mile territorial sea (Article 3), and distinguishes innocent passage by nonmilitary ships from permission for foreign military ships (Article 6). These are distinct zones and ship categories. The law alone does not establish the asserted geographic extent or a blanket foreign-ship prohibition. The cited 1996 declaration’s coordinates and the relevant internal-water access rules were not compared in this review; those remain necessary for the full claim. Rechecked November 14, 2026. Annex 1 of the State Department study reproduces the May 1996 declaration, which expressly covers part of the mainland-adjacent coast and separately lists the Paracels. Its geographic scope is narrower than an already complete coastwide system. Distinguish the 1992 statutory method, the baselines declared as of the paper's date, and navigation rights in the relevant waters.
evidence: PRC Law on the Territorial Sea and Contiguous Zone, Articles 2, 3, 6 and 15
May 15, 1996 declaration reproduced in Limits in the Seas No. 117, annex 1

rows.source: South China Sea sovereignty wording and distinct maritime rights
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMS13-S8N006: An official’s 2011 comments suggest China seeks indisputable sovereignty over South China Sea waters inside the nine-dashed line.
rows.finding: Reviewed November 11, 2026. Indonesia’s July 8, 2010 UN note reproduces China’s May 7, 2009 formulation: sovereignty over islands and adjacent waters, alongside sovereign rights and jurisdiction over relevant waters and seabed. Those legal categories cannot simply be treated as sovereignty over every enclosed water area. The specific September 15, 2011 Economic Times quotation and underlying MFA transcript were not retrieved, so the unnamed official’s broader formulation remains unverified. The reproduced 2009 wording provides partial context, not a refutation of an unread 2011 statement. Rechecked November 14, 2026. The September 15 official transcript identifies the spokesperson as Jiang Yu. She associates sovereignty with the Nansha Islands and adjacent waters, while addressing rights and other claims separately. The original transcript supports that attribution and narrower description. The inference of sovereignty over all waters within the dashed line is unsupported by this answer.
evidence: Indonesian UN note No. 480/POL-703/VII/10, paragraph 2 reproducing the Chinese formulation
PRC MFA transcript, Jiang Yu, September 15, 2011, South China Sea questions

rows.source: The 2010 strategy’s just international order formulation

rows.source: Article 38 identifies sources but does not expressly rank their importance
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CMS13-S8N027: Note 27 describes conventional and customary law as the generally recognized most important sources of international law.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** Article 38 expressly lists treaties, custom and general principles, with decisions and scholarship as subsidiary means. The ILC discussion confirms that structural distinction. Neither provision ranks the first three by practical importance. The chapter’s statement that treaties and custom are generally recognized as most important is commentary whose cited manual passage remains unrecovered.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** The exact cited manual pages and the scope of their comparative claim.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Reviewed November 11, 2026. Article 38(1) lists international conventions, international custom, general principles, and, subject to Article 59, judicial decisions and publicists as subsidiary means. It confirms conventions and custom are sources, but does not expressly declare the first two most important. That evaluative proposition requires the cited Brownlie and Damrosch passages, which were not retrieved. This audit is limited to Note 27; it does not verify Note 53’s persistent-objector claim in the same consolidated row. Rechecked November 14, 2026. The ILC’s 2023 report expressly describes Article 38 as its authoritative starting point and separates subsidiary means from primary sources. It still supplies no express ranking of treaties and custom above general principles. The finding is confined to the note’s evaluative claim pending its cited manuals. Follow-up review, November 14, 2026. The official ICJ text identifies treaty and custom alongside general principles. It expressly labels judicial decisions and scholarly writings subsidiary means. A claim of relative importance between the first three is commentary and still needs the cited manual pages. Follow-up review, November 15, 2026. The ICJ statute presents decisions and scholarship as subsidiary means, while it lists general principles alongside treaties and custom. That structural distinction supplies a defensible limited comparison. The text cannot settle the cited authors’ comparative ranking of treaties and custom.
evidence: Statute of the International Court of Justice, Article 38
ILC report chapter VII, Article 38 discussion

paper_memo.memo_title: Audit Memo: Beyond the Wall — Chinese Far Seas Operations (Dutton & Martinson, eds., 2015)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: China Maritime Study No. 13 collects ten papers from a 2013 PLA Navy–U.S. Navy scholars' dialogue and a 2012 CMSI conference on China's far seas operations. Its shared premise is that a redistribution of power is under way, that the U.S. Navy will stay dominant but needs help with nontraditional threats, and that U.S.–China naval cooperation (as shown in the Gulf of Aden) could improve the broader relationship, even though the two sides differ on whether to emphasize rules or relationships.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Introduction (Dutton & Martinson)**: Origins of the dialogue and the rules-versus-relationships contrast.
• **Ch. 1–3 (Rielage; Wu Zhengyu; Xu Qiyu)**: Multipolarity, land–sea balance and the stability of the maritime domain.
• **Ch. 4–5 (Erickson & Strange; Zhang Junshe)**: PLAN antipiracy escorts and U.S.–China cooperation.
• **Ch. 6 (Yung)**: Six overseas basing models.
• **Ch. 7 (Cai Penghong)**: China's overseas interests and 'peaceful competition.'
• **Ch. 8 (Odom)**: Law of the sea and far-seas freedom.
• **Ch. 9 (Wang Xiaoxuan)**: SLOC security and international cooperation.
• **Ch. 10 (Redden & Saunders)**: The U.S.–China maritime dynamic and EEZ military activities.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Concepts**: *far seas / distant seas (远海)*, *multipolarity*, *sea-lane security*, *rimland powers*, *pit stop*, *lean colonial network*, *dual-use logistics facility*, *string of pearls*, *peaceful competition*, *new type of great-power relationship*, *Military Maritime Consultative Agreement (MMCA)*.
• **Quantitative claims**: nineteen task forces, `15,000` personnel, `~6,000` ships (end 2014); `>6,000` ships, `15` flotillas, `40` warships, `32` helicopters (August 2013); China–Africa trade `$10bn → $127bn` (2000–10); `5.1 mbd` crude imports (2011) versus `~20%` of consumption; foreign trade `47%` of GDP (2012), `80–90%` by sea.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 8 reference rows audited in `CMS-13`, 3 are rated `ok`, 3 are rated `unk` and 2 are rated `fix`:
• **`[CMS13-R02]` (`fix` — Escort Totals)**: Zhang's August 2013 figure of more than six thousand ships exceeds the end-2014 total in Chapter 4.
• **`[CMS13-R06]` (`fix` — Oil and Trade Dependence)**: Cai's 20 percent oil-import share and 10 percent seaborne-trade share conflict with data elsewhere in the volume.
• **`[CMS13-R04]`, `[CMS13-R05]`, `[CMS13-R08]` (`unk`)**: Investment figures of unclear basis, a basing forecast and positional legal arguments.

The volume is **the clearest record of the 2013–15 U.S.–China naval dialogue on far-seas operations** and a comparison with work on Djibouti, overseas logistics and EEZ friction (`CMR-06` in 2020, `CMS-07` in 2010 and `CMS-10` in 2013). The last two precede this 2015 volume. Its limits are its conference-proceedings character, the mix of Chinese official and independent voices, and the uneven quality of its statistics.

**Footnote rows**: all 254 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 197 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMS13-S1N001 to CMS13-S10N033). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 254 notes: 85 (33%) are confirmed, 0 of them against a retrieved source and 85 after an outside web search (70 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 7 are flagged for reader check; 169 (67%) are not confirmed. Of the 169 notes not confirmed, 26 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 33 were judged not web-checkable (8 the authors' own data, imagery or analysis; 2 private interviews or conversations; 15 print-only books or paywalled items; 5 notes that are explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation; 3 other items); 110 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 197 source rows are 63 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 134 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMS13-S3N011`: The sentence says Thailand's later joining in this initiative (the Malacca Straits Patrols) led to "eyes in the sky" patrols to enhance coordinated aerial surveillance; `CMS13-S4N004`: The sentence says the PLAN was almost certain to continue its contributions following the announcement in late 2014 that the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force would take command of the international antipiracy force, citing a Kyodo item dated 18 [month] 2014. The searches find the first report in July 2014 (Japan Times), the…; `CMS13-S8N029`: The sentence says freedoms of the seas have included the collecting of intelligence and conducting of surveillance by militaries, citing Clinton's letter of transmittal; and 4 more. 63 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

sections.heading: Open claim-audit follow-up, November 22, 2026 (review complete; gaps recorded)
sections.body:
This continuation targets 7 initially open claim audits in this paper. 7 have a recorded individual follow-up: 0 now have a supported or correction finding; 7 remain unresolved. 0 of this paper’s initial open audits still await this continuation. Every reviewed row retains its evidence limits; a completed follow-up does not mean every substantive claim is verified.

[CMS13-R04](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-13&row=CMS13-R04): Reviewed; unresolved. The original 2010 company-population denominator and MOFCOM passage behind the 22-percent figure; the underlying methodology of the attributed worker estimate remains distinct from verifying its quotation.

[CMS13-R05](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-13&row=CMS13-R05): Reviewed; unresolved. A defined comparison framework and dated evidence about the actual facilities if the six-model prediction is to be tested.

[CMS13-R08](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-13&row=CMS13-R08): Reviewed; unresolved. Original attributed passages where translation is at issue, and an explicit comparison sample for the national approaches generalization.

[CMS13-R14](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-13&row=CMS13-R14): Reviewed; unresolved. A matched historical all-mode trade dataset and explicit volume/value definition for the stated range.

[CMS13-R26](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-13&row=CMS13-R26): Reviewed; unresolved. The exact cited manual pages and the scope of their comparative claim.

[CMS13-R30](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-13&row=CMS13-R30): Reviewed; unresolved. A full dated search summary with identical cutoff, vessel classifications, the additional participant counts and surveyed-area definition.

[CMS13-R31](#audit?type=claim&paper=CMS-13&row=CMS13-R31): Reviewed; unresolved. The exact cited speech/2013 statement and a clearly attributed interpretation of their implications; no U.S. undertaking is verified.

rows.source: PLAN Missile Fast-Attack Craft and Amphibious Ship Numbers: 'About Eighty-Six' FACs with About 70 Percent Type 022 (Pentagon 'Roughly Eighty-Five' with Sixty Type 022; Military Balance 2013 Over 100 Including Sixty-Five Type 022); MB 1996/97 'About 185' (Some 100 Huangfeng, About 75 Houku, Nine Houxin, One Huang) (Chapter 1)
rows.usage: Provides the baseline for the decline in numbers and rise in quality of PLAN missile craft.
rows.finding: The arithmetic is consistent: 100 + 75 + 9 + 1 = 185, and 60 of about 86 is about 70 percent. The competing counts (85 or over 100) are reported as source differences by the author rather than reconciled, so the 86 figure is an estimate.

rows.source: Type 022 Houbei Characteristics Across Chapters: 220 Tons and Eight YJ-8A of 50 nm (Chapter 1) versus 250 Tons and Eight C-803 (Chapter 2) versus Eight YJ-83 of 100 nm (Chapter 4); Counts of 60/65 (Chapter 1), 'More Than Sixty' 2004–08 (Chapter 4), 'Roughly Seventy' Through 2013 with Up to 100 Planned (Chapter 6)
rows.usage: Characterizes the PLAN's most numerous modern surface combatant class.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The chapters' displacement, weapon-label, range and fleet-count observations are estimates drawn at potentially different dates and using different category conventions. They should not be fused into one composite specification or treated as mutually exclusive without identifying full-load versus other displacement measures. The earlier chapter's 250-ton wording is present in the supplied text. The conflicting figures and forecasted total remain unreconciled; no independently comparable original class and hull account was recovered here.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** Each chapter's original source, date and measurement convention, and a common-date hull inventory for the count comparison.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** The chapters give different displacement, missile type and range, and fleet-size figures for the same class and the editors do not reconcile them (`unk`); the counts also differ from the 83 Type 022 in the CMS-11 fleet table, so no single figure is established by this volume.

rows.source: Amphibious Fleet Count: Pentagon 2013 Lists Fifty-Five Medium and Large Ships (3 LPD, 26 LST, 26 LSM); Military Balance 2013 Lists Eighty-Seven (2 LPD, 26 LST, 59 LSM); About Five of Twenty-Eight Type 079 LSMs Remain, Leaving a Gap of Twenty-Three (Chapter 1, Table 3)
rows.usage: Shows how much counts of the PLAN's amphibious fleet depend on what is included.
rows.finding: Both totals sum correctly (3 + 26 + 26 = 55; 2 + 26 + 59 = 87) and 28 − 5 = 23; subtracting those 23 from 87 gives 64, which is closer to the Pentagon's 55 but not 'close,' and the author does not reconcile the remaining nine-ship gap or the LPD count (two versus three).

rows.source: McDevitt's Type 052 Series Counts: Luhu Two, Luhai One, Luyang I Two, Luyang II 'Eight Ships,' Luyang III One Commissioned and Up to Twelve Planned; First Two 052C in 2004–05, 'Eight-Year Hiatus,' Four 052C Launched Since 2010; Sixteen Luda in 1971–91 Plus Two Luhu Equal Eighteen Destroyers (Chapter 5)
rows.usage: Quantifies the build-up of the PLAN's modern destroyer force.
rows.finding: Internal inconsistency (`fix`): two 052Cs commissioned in 2004–05 plus four launched since 2010 make six, not eight, which matches Nan Li's account of two launched in 2003 and four new hulls from late 2010 and Koda's projected six by 2020; the 16 Luda + 2 Luhu = 18 sum is consistent. Class designations also differ between chapters (Luhu is Type 052 in McDevitt but Type 052A, commissioned 2004, in Koda).

rows.source: Koda's 2020 Projections by Fleet from Sekai no Kansen (March 2013): NSF Six Destroyers and Five Frigates; ESF Ten Destroyers and Sixteen Frigates (Ten/Thirty-six = 28 Percent, 26/42 = 62 Percent of the JMSDF); SSF 'Eight Destroyers and Twelve Frigates' with 'Six Total Luyang II and III' (Tables 1–4, Chapter 3)
rows.usage: Projects relative PLAN, JMSDF and ROK surface-force strength to 2020.
rows.finding: The NSF and ESF numbers and the 28 and 62 percent ratios check out, but the South Sea Fleet figures do not (`fix`): Table 3 sums to nine destroyers (2 + 2 + 5) and Table 4 lists 9 DDs, not the eight in the text, and Luyang II plus III in Table 3 total seven, not six; Tables 1–3 also place the Type 052D in the frigate rows. The numbers are a Japanese publication's 2013 estimate, not observed 2020 force levels.

rows.source: First Type 052D Destroyer Named Changchun (150), Commissioned 31 January 2013, Followed by the Type 056 Frigate Bengbu (582) Commissioned 12 March 2013; Liaoning Commissioned 25 September 2012 (Chapter 6)
rows.usage: Dates the arrival of the PLAN's newest escort classes for carrier groups.
rows.finding: Conflicts with other chapters (`fix`): Koda records that a 'new ship (DD 150)' was commissioned in 2013 as the resumption of Luyang II construction and that the first Luyang III (052D) was commissioned in early 2014, and McDevitt also lists only one 052D commissioned; hull 150 is therefore a Type 052C, not the first 052D. The Liaoning date matches the chapter's other mentions.

rows.source: Auxiliary Fleet: Six Type 903/903A Fuchi-Class Replenishment Ships (Two in 2004–05, Four in 2011–15); Peace Ark (Anwei) 23,369 Tons; Flottes de Combat 2012: China Second in Tonnage with Eighteen Major Auxiliaries (206,930 Tons) versus Russia's Forty-One (203,020 Tons) and the U.S. Thirty-five (494,360 Tons) (Chapter 8, Notes)
rows.usage: Measures whether the PLAN's support ships can sustain far-seas operations.
rows.finding: The counts reconcile (2 + 4 = 6 Fuchi, matching the stated four additional ships in 2013–16) and the ranking by tonnage is consistent with the figures quoted, though China's eighteen ships average about 11,500 tons versus Russia's roughly 5,000; the order-of-battle tables by fleet are partly unreadable in the PDF and were not used to count vessels.

rows.source: PLAN Logistics Reform: 2007 CMC 'Outline for Building Modern Logistics in an All-Around Way'; Fleet Logistics Departments Established in Late 2011 (Disestablished 1985 by Liu Huaqing); 244 Billeting Projects in Sixty-three Units; 1,600 Housing Units Reclaimed; Vice Adm. Wang Shouye Arrested 2006, Sentenced to Death, Later Commuted to Life (Chapter 9)
rows.usage: Documents the organizational and corruption-control changes behind PLAN sustainment.
rows.finding: The Wang Shouye case matches contemporaneous reporting (removal in 2006; a suspended death sentence later reported as life imprisonment; the chapter omits the reprieve); the other items rest on PLAN newspapers (People's Navy, PLA Daily) that were not retrieved here but are internally consistent. The 1985 reform attributed to Liu Huaqing matches the Liu Huaqing material already in the corpus.

rows.source: Why the Surface Fleet Matters: Nan Li's 'Balanced Development' and 'Information Systems-Based System-of-Systems Operations' (Hu Jintao 2005); Rubel on the Limits of Leapfrogging and Carrier 'Senility'; Blasko's 'Yin and Yang' of Offshore Defense and Far-Seas Tasks (Chapters 1, 4 and 7)
rows.usage: Explains the doctrinal and conceptual drivers of the surface fleet's growth and the prospects of carrier aviation.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** Rubel's carrier-senility discussion on the supplied PDF p. 101 is explicitly an analytical thought experiment. It should not be presented as a demonstrated obsolescence finding. Nan Li's doctrinal reading and Blasko's mapping of offshore and far-seas tasks are different interpretive components with their own sources. No independent evidence supplied here proves a future force outcome or the relative causal weight of those doctrines. The arguments remain useful when attributed with their assumptions and limits intact.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** Original doctrinal wording for the source-attribution components and an explicit evidence-based test for any claimed future outcome.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** These are interpretive arguments (`unk`): Nan Li's account depends on PLA analysts' writings not retrieved here, Rubel's carrier-senility discussion is explicitly a thought experiment, and Blasko's missions mapping reflects his reading of PLA doctrine and white papers (2000 and 2013).

rows.usage: The note is attached to: “In October 2011, Anwei embarked on a three-month deployment to the Caribbean—Mission Harmony 2011—involving port calls in Cuba, Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago, and Costa Rica.”

rows.source: Changchun commissioning: Type 052C, not Type 052D
rows.usage: The note is attached to: “To augment further its surface vessels to meet escort requirements for an aircraft carrier task force, the PLAN commissioned the first of its Type 052D airdefense destroyers, named Changchun (150), on January 31, 2013.”
rows.finding: Xinhua’s account explicitly identifies Changchun, hull 150, as a Type 052C commissioned on January 31, 2013. The ship name, hull and date align; the Type 052D label does not. Correct the class identification and remove the claim that this event commissioned the first Type 052D. This is an identity and chronology correction.

paper_memo.memo_title: Audit Memo: China's Evolving Surface Fleet (Dutton & Martinson, eds., 2017)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: China Maritime Study No. 14 gathers nine analyses of the PLAN's surface fleet, from fast-attack craft and amphibious ships to destroyers, carriers, auxiliaries and logistics. Its common thread is that a navy once built around coastal defense is acquiring modern surface combatants and support ships for far-seas missions, while the contributors differ on emphasis: Blasko on the 'yin and yang' of offshore and far-seas missions, McDevitt on the destroyer force, Koda on 2020 numbers, Nan Li on doctrine, Mehta on the Indian Ocean, Rubel on carrier aviation, Sheldon-Duplaix and Rielage on sustainment.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Chapter 1 (Blasko)**: Missile craft and amphibious ships.
• **Chapter 2 (Cole)**: Maritime strategy and the surface fleet.
• **Chapter 3 (Koda)**: A Japanese perspective and 2020 projections.
• **Chapter 4 (Nan Li)**: PLA doctrinal reasons for the surface fleet's importance.
• **Chapter 5 (McDevitt)**: The modern destroyer force.
• **Chapter 6 (Mehta)**: Roles in the Indian Ocean region.
• **Chapter 7 (Rubel)**: Carrier aviation.
• **Chapter 8 (Sheldon-Duplaix)**: The auxiliary fleet.
• **Chapter 9 (Rielage)**: Logistics and maintenance.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Concepts**: *offshore defense (近海防御)*, *far seas (远海)*, *balanced development*, *information systems-based system-of-systems operations (基于信息系统的体系作战)*, *comprehensive support base*, *military operations other than war*, *carrier senility*.
• **Quantitative claims**: FACs `~86` (`~70%` Type 022); MB 1996/97 `185` missile craft; amphibious ships `55` (DoD) versus `87` (MB 2013); Type 052C `8` (McDevitt) versus `6` (computed); Koda 2020: NSF `6 DD/5 FF`, ESF `10 DD/16 FF`, SSF `8` versus `9 DD`/`12 FF`; Fuchi `6`; auxiliary tonnage `206,930`; fleet logistics departments `late 2011`; `244` billeting projects.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 9 reference rows audited in `CMS-14`, 4 are rated `ok`, 2 are rated `unk` and 3 are rated `fix`:
• **`[CMS14-R04]` (`fix` — Type 052C Count)**: Eight ships in the class versus six computed from McDevitt's own account.
• **`[CMS14-R05]` (`fix` — Koda SSF Projection)**: Text and tables disagree on the South Sea Fleet's 2020 destroyers.
• **`[CMS14-R06]` (`fix` — First 052D)**: Hull 150 is named as the first Type 052D but is treated elsewhere as a Luyang II.
• **`[CMS14-R02]`, `[CMS14-R09]` (`unk`)**: Houbei specifications that differ across chapters and interpretive doctrinal claims.

The volume is **a valuable multi-author snapshot of the PLAN surface fleet circa 2013–15**, bridging the earlier near-seas volume (`CMS-11`) and later work on the Type 055 and Djibouti (`CMR-05`, `CMR-06`). Its limits are the lack of reconciliation between chapters, reliance on third-party order-of-battle sources and the datedness of its counts.

**Footnote rows**: all 286 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 213 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMS14-S2N001 to CMS14-S20N046). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 286 notes: 67 (23%) are confirmed, 3 of them against a retrieved source and 64 after an outside web search (48 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 12 are flagged for reader check; 219 (77%) are not confirmed. Of the 219 notes not confirmed, 65 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 29 were judged not web-checkable (5 the authors' own data, imagery or analysis; 2 private interviews or conversations; 11 print-only books or paywalled items; 6 notes that are explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation; 5 other items); 125 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 213 source rows are 45 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 168 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMS14-S2N037`: The sentence lists B, G, N, J or S as the military-region letters; the Jamestown China Brief page (Blasko, 19 Aug 2010) lists G, N, J and S only, in its note 15. The paper may draw B from another source or later work; that was not retrieved; `CMS14-S5N008`: The sentence says the U.S. Navy stopped, boarded and inspected Soviet cargo ships carrying missiles to Cuba. Sources found describe the boarding of the Marucla (Lebanese flag, Soviet charter), the Navy coming alongside other ships and letting them pass, and some Soviet ships passing the line unstopped; `CMS14-S5N023`: The sentence says China's naval strategy has integrated the new concept of "far-seas operations" since the middle of the first decade of the twenty-first century; and 9 more. 61 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.
